front: Define force.
back:
A force is a push or a pull that acts on
an object due to the interaction with
another object. Forces can cause
changes in speed, direction, or shape of
bodies.

front:
True or False?
Balanced forces produce a resultant
force.
back:
False.
Unbalanced forces produce a resultant
force.

front: What is a resultant force?
back:
A resultant force is a single force that
represents the combined effect of all
forces acting on an object. It determines
both the direction and the magnitude
of the overall force experienced by the
object.

front:
State the two possible outcomes when
forces combine.
back:
Forces can combine to produce either
balanced or unbalanced forces.

front: Define balanced forces.
back:
Balanced forces occur when the forces
acting on an object are equal in
magnitude and opposite in direction,
resulting in no net force acting on the
object.

front: When do unbalanced forces occur?
back:
Unbalanced forces occur when the
forces acting on an object are unequal
in magnitude or not opposite in
direction, resulting in a net force that
causes the object to accelerate in the
direction of the net force.

front:
An object is travelling forward at a
constant speed in a straight line. A force
is applied perpendicular to the direction
of the object's motion. What is the
effect of the force on the object's
motion?
back:
If a force is applied perpendicularly to
the direction of an object's motion, the
object will change direction.

front:
An object is travelling forward at a
constant speed in a straight line. What
is the effect on the object's motion if a
forward acting force is applied?
back:
If a forward acting force is applied to an
object travelling at a constant speed in a
straight line, the object will speed up
(accelerate).

front:
True or False?
Newton's first law states that objects
will continue to move at the same
velocity even if a resultant force acts
on them.
back:
False.
Newton's first law states that objects
will continue to move at the same
velocity when there is no resultant
force acting on them.

front:
What is the effect of a zero resultant
force on an object's motion?
back:
The effect of a zero resultant force on
the motion of an object is that the
object will:
remain stationary if it is at rest
continue to move with the same
velocity if it is already moving

front:
How is Newton's first law applied to
objects with constant velocity?
back:
Newton's first law states that objects
with constant velocity will experience no
change in their motion unless a
resultant force is applied.

front: Define constant velocity.
back:
Constant velocity refers to motion at a
steady speed and in a straight line.

front:
In what situation does an object
experience no resultant force?
back:
The situation when an object
experiences no resultant force when
the forces acting on it are balanced,
meaning the net force is zero.

front:
What is the value of the frictional force
on a car moving at a constant velocity
with no external forces acting on it?
back:
The value of the frictional force is equal
to the driving force, as both forces are
balanced when the car moves at a
constant velocity.

front: State Newton's first law of motion.
back:
Newton's first law of motion states that:
objects will remain at rest, or move with
a constant velocity unless acted on by a
resultant force.

front:
When a non-zero resultant force is
applied to an object, what are the two
possible changes in the object's
motion?
back:
When a non-zero force acts on an
object, the object can:
change its speed
change its direction

front:
Define Newton's second law of
motion.
back:
Newton's second law of motion states
that the acceleration of an object is
proportional to the resultant force
acting on it and inversely proportional
to the object's mass.

front:
True or False?
Newton's second law states that
acceleration is directly proportional to
the object's mass. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Newton's second law states that
acceleration is directly proportional to
the object's resultant force, and
inversely proportional to its mass.

front:
How does Newton's second law build
on Newton's first law ?
back:
Newton's first law states that an object's
motion will change if acted upon by a
resultant force, and Newton's second
law describes that change in motion.

front:
What is the equation for Newton's
second law? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The equation for Newton's second law
is F = ma
Where:
F = resultant force, measured in
Newtons (N)
m = mass, measured in kilograms
(kg)
a = acceleration, measured in
metres per second squared (m/s2)

front:
True or False?
In the equation F = ma , the force and
acceleration act in opposite directions.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
In the equation F = ma , the force and
acceleration act in the same direction.

front:
State the relationship between mass
and acceleration according to
Newton's second law. (Extended Tier
Only) experience smaller accelerations for the
back:
According to Newton's second law,
acceleration is inversely proportional
to mass, meaning a larger mass will
same applied force.

front:
According to Newton's second law,
increasing the resultant force acting on
an object will have what effect on its
acceleration? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
According to Newton's second law,
increasing the resultant force acting on
an object will increase the acceleration
of the object by the same factor.

front:
True or False?
According to Newton's second law, the
acceleration of an object is inversely
proportional to its mass. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
True.
According to Newton's second law, the
acceleration of an object is inversely
proportional to its mass.

front:
Define Hooke's Law. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Hooke’s law states that the extension
of a spring is proportional to the applied
force.

front:
What is the equation for Hooke's law?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The equation for Hooke's law is F = kx
Where:
F = force applied, measured in
newtons (N)
k = spring constant, measured in
newtons per kilogram (N/m)
x = extension of the spring,
measured in metres (m)

front:
True or False?
Hooke's Law states that the extension
of a spring is inversely proportional to
the applied force. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Hooke's Law states that the extension
of a spring is directly proportional to
the applied force.

front:
What does Hooke's Law describe?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Hooke's Law describes the relationship
between the extension of a spring and
the applied force, stating that they are
proportional.

front:
What is the spring constant in Hooke's
Law? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The spring constant (k) is the force per
unit extension and measures how stiff
the spring is.

front:
True or False?
The spring constant (k) has units of
N/kg. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
The spring constant (k) has units of
N/m.

front:
What does the elastic limit represent
in Hooke's Law? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The elastic limit represents the point
beyond which an object will no longer
return to its original length when
stretched, violating Hooke's Law.

front:
What does the green arrow represent
on this force-extension graph?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The green arrow shows the linear
portion of the graph. This is the section
that obeys Hooke's law, where force
and extension are directly
proportional.

front:
What does the green arrow represent
on this force-extension graph?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The green arrow shows the non-linear
section of the graph where Hooke's law
is not obeyed. Force and extension are
no longer proportional.

front:
What does the red cross represent on
this force-extension graph? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
The red cross represents the limit of
proportionality. Beyond this point, force
and extension are no longer directly
proportional.

front:
Define circular motion. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Circular motion is the movement of an
object along a circular path, where the
object's velocity is constantly changing
due to the change in direction.

front:
True or False?
In circular motion, an object's speed
and velocity remain constant.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
In circular motion, an object's speed
may be constant, but its velocity is
constantly changing due to the change
in direction.

front:
What happens to an object's velocity in
circular motion? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
In circular motion, an object's velocity is
always changing as it moves along the
circular path.

front:
How does a force cause an object to
change direction in circular motion?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
A force causes an object to change
direction in circular motion when it acts
at 90 degrees to the direction of travel.

front:
What factors determine the force
needed to maintain circular motion?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The factors that determine the force
needed to maintain circular motion
depend on the mass of the object, the
speed of the object, and the radius of
the circular path.

front:
True or False?
A smaller radius of the circular path
requires a smaller force to maintain
circular motion at constant speed.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
A smaller radius requires a greater
force to maintain constant speed in
circular motion.

front:
True or False?
Velocity is defined as the rate of
change of displacement. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
True.
Velocity is defined as the rate of
change of displacement.

front:
What two factors are affected by the
size of the radius of an object in
circular motion? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The two factors that are affected by the
size of the radius of an object in circular
motion are how large the circular path
is and the force required to maintain
the motion.

front:
True or False?
A satellite orbiting a planet is an
example of circular motion.
back:
True.
A satellite orbiting a planet is an
example of circular motion.

front:
True or False?
The speed of an object in circular
motion will increase if the force is
increased providing that the mass and
radius remain constant.
back:
True.
The speed of an object in circular
motion will increase if the force is
increased providing that the mass and
radius remain constant.

front:
True or False?
The radius of an object in circular
motion will increase if the force is
increased providing that the mass and
speed remain constant.
back:
False.
The radius of an object in circular
motion will decrease if the force is
increased providing that the mass and
speed remain constant.

front:
True or False?
For an object in circular motion, an
increased mass requires an increased
force to keep the speed and radius
constant.
back:
True.
For an object in circular motion, an
increased mass requires an increased
force to keep the speed and radius
constant.

front: Define friction.
back:
Friction is the force between two
surfaces that impedes motion and
produces heating.

front:
True or False?
Friction speeds up the motion of an
object.
back:
False.
Friction opposes the motion of an
object, slowing it down.

front:
True or False?
Friction increases the temperature of
an object.
back:
True.
Friction causes heating, which raises the
temperature of the object and its
surroundings.

front:
What creates friction between two solid
objects?
back:
Friction in solids is created by
imperfections on the surfaces of the
objects moving over one another.

front: Define fluids .
back:
Fluids are substances that can flow and
take the shape of their container.
Gases and liquids are fluids.

front: Define drag.
back:
Drag is the frictional force acting on
objects moving through fluids, caused
by collisions with the gas or liquid
particles.

front:
True or False?
Air resistance is a type of friction.
back:
True.
Air resistance, experienced by objects
moving through the air, is a type of
friction that slows down their motion.

front:
How does air resistance affect the
temperature of an object?
back:
Air resistance increases the
temperature of an object by heating
due to the work done against
frictional forces as particles collide
with the object.

front:
True or False?
Drag is a type of friction.
back:
True.
Drag is the frictional force acting on an
object as the object moves through a
fluid (a liquid or a gas).

front:
What is the primary energy source for
most of Earth's energy resources?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The primary source of energy for most
of Earth's energy resources is the Sun.

front:
True or False?
The Sun heats up the atmosphere,
creating wind and producing waves.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
The Sun heats up the atmosphere,
creating wind and producing waves.

front:
True or False?
Geothermal is an energy form that
comes from the Sun. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
False.
Geothermal is an energy form that
comes from the heating of rocks by the
Earth's core and not from the Sun.

front: What are solar cells?
back:
Solar cells, also known as photovoltaic
cells, are devices made of
semiconducting materials that produce
electricity from sunlight in a process
called the photoelectric effect.

front:
True or False?
Solar energy is a renewable resource.
back:
True.
Solar energy is considered renewable
because it is derived from the Sun
which is expected to continue shining
for billions of years.

front:
How is solar energy transferred to the
Earth?
back:
Solar energy is transferred to the Earth
by radiation, in the form of visible light
and infrared radiation.

front:
True or False?
Solar panels produce greenhouse gases
and pollution.
back:
False.
Solar panels produce no greenhouse
gases or pollution once they are
operating.

front: What are solar panels?
back:
Solar panels are devices that transfer
energy from sunlight to the thermal
store of the panels, which is then used
to heat water.

front:
What are the main advantages of solar
energy?
back:
Advantages of solar energy include:
renewable
reliable in hot climates
produce no greenhouse gases or
pollution
Can be used in remote areas

front:
How do solar furnaces generate
electricity?
back:
Solar furnaces consist of large curved
mirrors that focus sunlight onto a small
area, which heats water to produce
steam, which then turns turbines which
generate electricity.

front:
True or False?
Solar farms need to be small-scale to
produce large amounts of electricity.
back:
False.
Solar farms need to be large-scale to
produce significant amounts of
electricity.

front: What are fossil fuels?
back:
Fossil fuels are natural resources
formed over millions of years from the
remains of plants and animals.

front: What are the three main fossil fuels?
back:
The three main fossil fuels are:
coal
oil
natural gas (methane)

front:
True or False?
Burning fossil fuels produces only
carbon dioxide.
back:
False.
Burning fossil fuels produces carbon
dioxide which is a greenhouse gas that
contributes to global warming. But
other harmful gases are also released in
the combustion of fossil fuels, such as
sulphur dioxide which causes acid
rain.

front:
What is a disadvantage of using fossil
fuels?
back:
The disadvantages of using fossil fuels
include:
non-renewable (so will run out)
produce carbon dioxide which
contributes to global warming
produce sulphur dioxide which
causes acid rain

front: What are the main uses of fossil fuels?
back:
The main uses of fossil fuels are
transportation, electricity
generation, and heating in homes and
industries.

front:
True or False?
It takes millions of years for fossil fuels
to form.
back:
True.
It takes millions of years for fossil fuels
to form. This is why they are considered
a non-renewable energy resource.

front:
What energy store is energy transferred
from in the combustion of fossil fuels?
back:
Energy is transferred from the chemical
store of the fossil fuel during
combustion. This energy originally came
from sunlight and was transferred to
plants and animals through
photosynthesis.

front: How are biofuels produced?
back:
Biofuels are produced from plant
matter, such as crops, which undergo
processes like fermentation or
distillation to extract ethanol or
methane for use as alternative fuels to
fossil fuels.

front:
What are the main advantage of using
biofuels?
back:
The main advantages of biofuels are:
renewable
carbon neutral

front:
True or False?
Nuclear power stations release no
pollution into the atmosphere during
normal operation.
back:
True.
Nuclear power stations do not release
pollution into the atmosphere during
normal operation.

front: What is nuclear fuel?
back:
Nuclear fuel refers to materials, such as
uranium, used in nuclear reactors to
release energy in nuclear fission
reactions.

front:
What is the process by which nuclear
power stations generate electricity?
back:
Nuclear power stations generate
electricity by using the energy released
in nuclear fission reactions to heat
water to produce steam. The steam
then turns turbines connected to
generators, which produce electricity.

front:
Why is nuclear fuel a non-renewable
resource?
back:
Nuclear fuel is a non-renewable
resource because there is a finite supply
of uranium ore found in the ground.

front:
Define power generation in terms of
wave and tide power.
back:
Wave and tide power harnesses the
energy from the rise and fall of waves or
tides to generate electricity, typically
using turbines.

front:
True or False?
Wave and tidal power produce
pollution.
back:
False.
Wave and tidal power do not produce
pollution.

front:
What is the primary advantages of
wave and tide power?
back:
The primary advantages of wave and
tide power are that they are renewable
energy resources that produce no
pollution.

front:
How do wave and tidal power stations
generate electricity?
back:
Wave and tidal power stations generate
electricity by utilising the motion of
waves or tides to turn turbines, which
then generate electricity through
electromagnetic induction.

front:
True or False?
Tidal barrages are suitable for large-
scale electricity production.
back:
False.
Tidal barrages are small systems that
produce small amounts of electricity.

front:
In terms of energy transfers, what is the
main purpose of the underwater
turbines in wave and tide power
systems?
back:
The main purpose of underwater
turbines in wave and tide power
systems is to transfer energy from the
kinetic store of the moving water to the
kinetic store of the turbines, which turn
generators that generate electricity.

front: What are hydroelectric dams?
back:
Hydroelectric dams are structures built
across rivers to store water at a height
in reservoirs. The water can be
released, flowing over a turbine that
turns a generator that generates
electricity.

front:
True or False?
Hydroelectric dams release large
amounts of greenhouse gases.
back:
True.
Hydroelectric dams can release
significant amounts of greenhouse
gases due to the decomposition of
organic matter in flooded areas, or due
to the fuels used to pump the water
back up to the reservoir.

front:
What is the main disadvantage of
hydroelectric dams?
back:
The main disadvantage of hydroelectric
dams is that they require valleys to be
flooded. This results in the destruction
of habitats, towns, and villages.

front:
What is the main advantage of
hydroelectric dams?
back:
The main advantage of hydroelectric
dams is their ability to respond to
electricity demand quickly and reliably.

front: What is geothermal energy?
back:
Geothermal energy is energy stored in
the thermal store of rocks beneath the
Earth's surface from tectonic heating.
The hot rocks are used to heat water
that can be used as a hot water supply
and to produce steam to turn turbines
for electricity generation.

front:
True or False?
Geothermal energy is a non-renewable
resource.
back:
False.
Geothermal energy is considered a
renewable resource.

front:
What is the primary advantage of
geothermal energy?
back:
The primary advantage of geothermal
energy is its reliability and
renewability. It offers a consistent
source of heating and electricity
production.

front:
What is the main disadvantage of
geothermal energy for electricity
production?
back:
The main disadvantage of geothermal
energy is the limited availability of
suitable locations for large-scale
electricity production.

front:
True or False?
Geothermal power stations are usually
large-scale facilities.
back:
False.
Geothermal power stations are typically
small compared to nuclear or fossil fuel
power stations due to the limited
availability of suitable geothermal sites.

front:
How does geothermal energy generate
electricity?
back:
Geothermal energy generates electricity
by heating water and generating steam
using the hot rocks beneath the Earth's
surface, which drives turbines to
produce electricity.

front:
What type of energy resource is
geothermal energy?
back:
Geothermal energy is a renewable
energy resource. This means it can be
replenished naturally and is sustainable
over the long term.

front:
What is the main advantage of
geothermal power stations?
back:
The main advantage of geothermal
power stations is their reliability as a
source of energy. They provide a
consistent and uninterrupted supply of
heat and electricity in suitable regions.

front:
Define nuclear fusion. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Nuclear fusion is the process by which
small nuclei, such as hydrogen, combine
to form larger nuclei, releasing a
massive amount of energy in the
process.

front:
True or False?
The Sun's energy source is nuclear
fission. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
The Sun's energy is released through
nuclear fusion reactions, where
hydrogen nuclei combine to form
helium nuclei, releasing massive
amounts of energy in the process.

front:
What is the primary advantage of
nuclear fusion? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The primary advantage of nuclear
fusion is its potential to provide virtually
limitless energy with minimal
environmental impact. It generates no
greenhouse gases and produces
minimal radioactive waste.

front:
What is the main challenge associated
with nuclear fusion. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
The main challenge associated with
nuclear fusion is the requirement of
extremely high temperatures and
pressures to initiate and sustain fusion
reactions, similar to those found in the
core of stars.

front:
True or False?
Fusion reactors are currently
operational for commercial electricity
generation. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Fusion reactors are still in the
experimental stage, and while progress
is being made, no fusion reactor has yet
achieved sustained net energy
production for commercial use.

front:
How does nuclear fusion differ from
nuclear fission? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Nuclear fusion involves the fusion of
small nuclei, such as hydrogen, to form
larger nuclei, while nuclear fission
involves the splitting of larger nuclei,
such as uranium, into smaller nuclei.

front:
What are scientists researching in
relation to fusion? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Scientists are researching methods to
sustain fusion reactions at lower
temperatures and pressures. This will
make fusion more practical for energy
generation on Earth.

front:
True or False?
Fusion reactions currently release more
energy than they consume. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
False.
Currently, fusion reactions require
nearly as much energy as they release.
Ongoing research aims to achieve
sustained net energy production in
fusion reactions.

front:
What is the potential impact of
successful fusion energy? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Successful fusion energy could
revolutionise global energy production,
providing a sustainable, carbon-free
source of electricity with virtually
unlimited fuel availability.

front: Define energy stores.
back:
Energy stores refer to the different ways in which
energy is stored in objects.

front:
True or False?
Energy is measured in units
of kilograms.
back:
False.
Energy is measured in units of joules (J).

front: Define a system in physics.
back: A system is an object or group of objects.

front:
True or False?
Magnetic and electrostatic
are examples of energy
stores used in physics.
back:
True.
Magnetic and electrostatic are examples of energy
stores used in physics. Other examples include
kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic, chemical,
nuclear, and thermal.

front:
True or False?
Objects have energy in
their elastic potential store
if they are stretched,
squashed or bent.
back:
True.
Objects have energy in their elastic potential store if
they are stretched, squashed or bent.

front:
True or False?
All objects have energy in
their thermal store, the
hotter the object, the less
energy it has in this store.
back:
False.
All objects have energy in their thermal store, the
hotter the object, the more energy it has in this
store.

front:
What is the definition of
energy transfer
pathways?
back:
Energy transfer pathways are the ways that energy
can be transferred from one energy store to
another.

front:
True or False?
Energy is transferred only
through mechanical
pathways.
back:
False.
Energy can be transferred through various
pathways, including mechanical, electrical, heating,
and radiation.

front:
Define mechanical
working in terms of energy
transfer.
back:
Mechanical work is the transfer pathway when a
force is exerted over a distance.

front:
True or False?
In a falling object, energy is
transferred from its kinetic
store to its gravitational
potential store.
back:
False.
In a falling object, energy is transferred from its
gravitational potential store to its kinetic store.

front:
State the four energy
transfer pathways used in
physics.
back:
The four energy transfer pathways used in physics
are:
mechanical
electrical
heating
radiation

front:
True or False?
An example of energy
transfer by heating is a hot
chocolate warming up cold
hands.
back:
True.
An example of energy transfer by heating is a hot
chocolate warming up cold hands.

front:
Define kinetic energy.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Kinetic energy is the energy an object possesses due
to its motion, determined by its mass and speed.

front:
True or False?
Any object in motion has
energy in its kinetic energy
store. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
Any object in motion possesses kinetic energy.

front:
What is the equation for
calculating kinetic energy?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The equation for calculating kinetic energy is
E = 1 mv 2
k 2
Where:
E k = kinetic energy, measured in joules (J)
m = mass, measured in kilograms (kg)
v = velocity, measured in metres per second
(m/s)

front:
True or False?
Kinetic energy is measured
in units of joules per
second. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
False.
Kinetic energy is measured in units of joules (J).

front:
What does the term v
represent in the kinetic
energy equation?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
In the kinetic energy equation, v represents the
speed of the object in meters per second (m/s).

front:
Define the term m in the
kinetic energy equation.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
In the kinetic energy equation, m represents the
mass of the object in kilograms (kg).

front:
How can kinetic energy be
calculated for a given
object? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Kinetic energy can be calculated by multiplying half
of the object's mass by the square of its speed.

front:
Define gravitational
potential energy.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Gravitational potential energy is the energy
possessed by an object due to its height in a
gravitational field.

front:
True or False?
Energy is transferred away
from an object's
gravitational potential
store when it is lifted.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Energy is transferred to an object's gravitational
potential store when it is lifted.

front:
What is the equation for
calculating gravitational
potential energy?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The equation for calculating gravitational potential
energy is ∆ E p = mg ∆ h
Where:
∆ E p = change in gravitational potential energy
m = mass, measured in kilograms (kg)
g = gravitational field strength, measured in
newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
∆ h = change in height in metres (m)

front:
True or False?
Gravitational potential
energy is measured in units
of newtons per kilogram
(N/kg). (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
False.
Gravitational potential energy is measured in units
of joules (J).

front:
What does the term m
represent in the
gravitational potential
energy equation?

Define g in terms of the

energy equation.

back:
In the gravitational potential energy equation, g
represents the gravitational field strength in
newtons per kilogram (N/kg).

front:
True or False?
Energy is transferred to an
object's gravitational
potential store when it
falls. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Energy is transferred away from an object's
gravitational potential store when it falls.

front:
True or False?
The total amount of energy
in a closed system can
change over time.
back:
False.
The total amount of energy in a closed system
remains constant; it cannot change over time
according to the principle of conservation of energy.

front:
What does an energy flow
diagram show?
back:
An energy flow diagram represents energy stores
and transfers within a system, showing both the
stores and the transfers taking place.

front:
For a system in which
energy is conserved, what
is an equation relating
wasted energy, total
energy in and useful
energy out?
back:
The equation representing the conservation of
energy is:
total energy in = useful energy out + wasted
energy

front:
What is a Sankey
diagram? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Sankey diagrams are graphical representations of
energy transfers, characterised by splitting arrows
that show the proportions of energy transfers taking
place.

The left-hand side of a Sankey diagram represents

wasted energy.

back:
The equation for calculating wasted energy is:
wasted energy = total energy in − useful energy out

front:
True or False?
Total energy in a closed
system equals useful
energy out plus wasted
energy. (Extended Tier

back:
True.
According to the principle of conservation of energy,
the total energy in a closed system is equal to the
useful energy out plus the wasted energy.

front:
Define mechanical work
done.
back:
Work done is the product of the force applied to an
object and the distance over which the force is
applied, measured in joules (J) or newton-metres (N
m).

front:
True or False?
Work is done when a force
is applied to an object,
regardless of whether the
object moves or not.
back:
False.
Work is done when a force is applied to an object
and results in the object's movement over a distance
in the direction of the force.

front:
What is the formula for
calculating work done?
back:
The formula for calculating work done is W = F × d
Where:
W = work done, measured in joules (J) or
newton metres (Nm)
F = force, measured in newtons (N)
d = distance, measured in metres (m)

front:
Define mechanical
working energy transfer.
back:
Mechanical working energy transfer is one form
of energy transfer when an object moves due to a
force acting on it.

front:
Define electrical working
energy transfer.
back:
Electrical working energy transfer is one form of
energy transfer when a charge moves through a
potential difference.

front:
True or False?
Work can only be done
mechanically.
back:
False.
Work can also be done electrically, by heating or by
radiation.

front:
True or False?
The amount of energy
transferred is equal to the
work done.
back:
True.
The amount of energy transferred (in joules) is equal
to the work done (in joules or newton-metres) when
any mechanical work is done.

front:
State the conversion
between joules and
newton metres.
back: 1 joule is equal to 1 newton metre

front:
State the relationship
between energy
transferred and work done.
back:
The relationship between energy transferred and
work done is:
energy transferred (J) = work done (J)

front:
True or False?
Work is done on a ball
when it is lifted to a height.
back:
True.
Work is done on a ball when it is lifted to a height.

front: Define power.
back:
Power is the rate at which energy is transferred or
work is done, measured in watts (W).

front:
True or False?
Power is the total amount
of energy transferred.
back:
False.
Power refers to the rate at which energy is
transferred or work is done, not the total amount of
energy transferred.

front:
True or False?
A car has more power if it
does the same amount of
work in a longer amount of
time.
back:
False.
A car has more power if it does the same amount of
work in a shorter amount of time.

back:

front:
Define the rate of doing
work.
back:
The rate of doing work, or power, refers to the
amount of work done or energy transferred per unit
time. It is measured in watts (W).

front:
True or False?
Power and work done are
the same quantities.
back:
False.
Power is the rate at which energy is transferred or
work is done, work done is the total amount of
energy transferred.

State the equation for
calculating energy

front:

Power is often measured in
joules (J).
back:
False.
Power is typically measured in watts (W), while
energy is measured in joules (J).

front: Define efficiency .
back:
Efficiency is a measure of the amount of useful
power or energy output from a system compared to
its total power or energy input. It is often expressed
as a percentage.

front:
True or False?
Efficiency is a measure of
how much useful energy is
wasted in an energy
transfer.
back:
True.
Efficiency measures how much power or energy is
transferred usefully, compared to the total power or
energy input. Therefore, it is also a measure of how
much energy or power is wasted.

front:
True or False?
The overall efficiency of a
typical coal-fired thermal
power station is 30%.
back:
True.
The overall efficiency of a typical coal-fired thermal
power station is 30%.

front:
True or False?
The higher the efficiency of
an energy transfer, the
more energy is wasted.
back:
False.
The higher the efficiency of an energy transfer, the
less energy is wasted.

front:
How is efficiency is
calculated?
back:
Efficiency is calculated as the ratio of useful power
or energy output to total power or energy input,
usually expressed as a percentage.

front:
State the equation for
calculating efficiency.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The equation for calculating efficiency is:
useful power or energy output
efficiency = total power or energy input × 100 %

front:
True or False?
Efficiency can be given in
both ratio and percentage
formats. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
Efficiency can be expressed as a ratio between 0 and
1, or as a percentage between 0 and 100%.

front:
True or False?
Efficiency has units.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Efficiency is a ratio and therefore a dimensionless
quantity that does not have any units.

front:
True or False?
If an energy transfer is 65%
efficient, then 35% of the
energy is wasted.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
If an energy transfer is 65% efficient, then 35% of the
energy is wasted.

front: Define mass.
back:
Mass is a measure of the quantity of
matter in an object at rest relative to
the observer.

front:
True or False?
Mass is a vector quantity.
back:
False.
Mass is a scalar quantity.

front:
The S.I. unit for mass is kg. What does
kg stand for?
back: The S.I. unit kg stands for kilograms.

front:
Define weight in terms of the effect of
a gravitational field. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Weight is the effect of a gravitational
field on an object with mass.

front: Define gravitational field strength
back:
Gravitational field strength is the force
. per unit mass acting on an object in a
gravitational field.

front:
True or False?
Weight is a measure of the quantity of
matter in an object. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
False.
Weight is a gravitational force on an
object with mass.

front:
True or False?
An object's mass varies depending on
the gravitational field strength
back:
False.
An object's mass is independent of
. gravitational field strength.

front:
What is the purpose of using a
balance?
back:
A balance is used to compare the
weights of two objects or to measure
the mass of an object.

front:
How is weight affected by the
gravitational field strength ?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Weight is affected by the gravitational
field strength; the stronger the
gravitational field , the greater the
weight of the object.

front: Define density.
back:
Density is defined as the mass per unit
volume of a material. It describes how
much mass is contained in a given
volume.

front:
True or False?
Objects made from high-density
materials typically have low mass.
back:
False.
Objects made from high-density
materials typically have a high mass.

back:
The units for density are grams per

measured in grams (g) and volume in
cubic centimetres (cm3).

front:
Why are gases generally less dense than
solids?
back:
Gases are generally less dense than
solids because the molecules in a gas
are more spread out over a larger
volume.

front:
True or False?
Density is a scalar quantity.
back:
True.
Density is a scalar quantity.

front: Define volume.
back:
Volume is the amount of space
occupied by an object in three-
dimensional space.

volume of an object.
back:
The equation used to calculate the

h = height of object, measured in

front:
Identify which object is more dense, the
one on the left or the one on the right.
back:
The object on the right is more dense
because the particles are packed more
closely together.

front: Define upthrust.
back:
Upthrust is a force that pushes
upwards on an object submerged in a
fluid (a liquid or a gas). It acts in the
opposite direction to the object's
weight and is caused by the pressure
difference between the top and
bottom of the object.

front:
True or False?
Upthrust always pushes downwards on
a submerged object.
back:
False.
Upthrust always pushes upwards on a
submerged object.

front:
What are the factors affecting whether
an object sinks or floats ?
back:
The factors affecting whether an object
sinks or floats are the upthrust it
experiences and its density.
If the upthrust is equal to or greater
than the object's weight, and if the
object's density is less than the density
of the fluid, it will float. Otherwise, it will
sink.

front:
A wooden block has a density of 0.9
g/cm3, and freshwater has a density of
1.0 g/cm3. Will the block sink or float in
freshwater?
back:
The wooden block will float because its
density is less than that of freshwater.

front:
How can you determine if one liquid will
float on top of another? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
To determine whether a liquid will float
on top of another, compare their
densities. The liquid with the lower
density will float on top of the one with
the higher density, assuming the liquids
do not mix.

front:
State the condition for liquid A to float
on liquid B.
back:
Liquid A will float on top of liquid B if
the density of liquid A is lower than
that of liquid B.

front:
True or False?
Density is always measured in
kilograms (kg).
back:
False.
Density mass per unit volume. The
units could be:
kilograms per metre cubed (kg/m3)
grams per centimetre cubed
(g/cm3)

front: Define a moment.
back:
A moment is the turning effect of a
force about a pivot.

front:
True or False?
Moments cause motion.
back:
False.
Moments do not cause motion, they
describe the turning effects due to
forces about a pivot. The resultant
force causes the motion.

What is the equation for calculating
moments?
back:
The equation used for calculating a
moment is M = F × d
Where:
M = moment, measured in newton
metres (Nm)
F = force, measured in newtons (N)
d = perpendicular distance to the
pivot, measured in metres (m)

front:
What does the size of a moment
depend upon?
back:
The size of a moment depends on both
the force applied and the
perpendicular distance to the pivot.

False.

front:
State the units for the moment of a
force.
back:
The units for the moment of a force are
newton metres (Nm).

True or False?
To reduce the force required to
produce a moment, the distance from
the pivot must be decreased.
back:
False.
To reduce the force required to produce
a moment, the distance from the pivot
must be increased.

front:
A force of 3 N is applied at a distance of
0.5 m from the pivot, what is the
moment of the force?
back:
When a force of 3 N is applied at a

moment of the force is 1.5 Nm.

True or False?
The principle of moments applies to
unbalanced systems.
back:
False.
The principle of moments specifically
applies to balanced systems.

front:
True or False?
The principle of moments describes a
system in equilibrium.
back:
True.
The principle of moments describes the
equilibrium condition in a balanced
system.

front:
True or False?
See-saws, beams and levers are
systems that use the principle of
moments.
back:
True.
See-saws, beams and levers are
systems that use the principle of
moments.

front:
Define equilibrium in terms of
moments.
back:
Equilibrium is a state in which an object
remains unchanged in its motion or
rotation, with balanced forces and
moments acting upon it.

front:
True or False?
In terms of moments, for an object to
be in equilibrium it must be stationary.
back:
False.
An object in equilibrium can either be
stationary or moving with constant
velocity.

front:
What does it mean for the forces on an
object to be balanced?
back:
When the forces on an object are
balanced, the net force acting on it is
zero, resulting in no change in its
motion.

front:
What condition must be met for there
to be no resultant force on an object?
back:
The condition that must be met for
there to be no resultant force on an
object is that the forces acting on it
must be balanced, cancelling each
other out.

front:
True or False?
In terms of moment, a system in
equilibrium has a net force acting on it.
back:
False.
A system in equilibrium has no net
force acting on it, so the net force is
zero.

front:
What is the significance of balanced
forces and moments in equilibrium
on a system?
back:
The significance of balanced forces and
moments in equilibrium on a system is
it remains unchanged in its state of
motion or rotation, maintaining
equilibrium.

front: Define the resultant moment.
back:
The resultant moment is the net
turning effect produced by the
combination of all forces acting on an
object, determining its rotational
motion.

front: Define the centre of gravity.
back:
The centre of gravity of an object is the
point at which the weight of the object
can be considered to act.

front:
True or False?
The centre of gravity is always located
at the geometric centre of an object.
back:
False.
The centre of gravity can be located at
the geometric centre of a regularly
shaped object. This is not necessarily
the case for irregularly shaped objects.

front:
True or False?
The location of the centre of mass of an
object affects its stability and balance.
back:
True.
The location of the centre of mass of
an object affects its stability and
balance.

front: Define stability.
back:
Stability refers to an object's ability to
maintain its equilibrium position,
where its centre of gravity lies above its
base.

front:
True or False?
An object is considered stable if its
centre of gravity is below its base.
back:
False.
An object is stable if its centre of gravity
lies above its base, ensuring balance
and preventing it from tipping over.

front:
How does the width of the base affect
an object's stability?
back:
The width of an object's base affects its
stability because a wider base lowers
the centre of gravity, increasing
stability, while a narrower base raises
it, decreasing stability.

front:
What factors influence an object's
stability?
back:
An object's stability is influenced by the
position of its centre of gravity and the
width of its base.

front:
State the condition required for an
object to be stable.
back:
An object is stable when its centre of
gravity is positioned above its base,
ensuring equilibrium and resistance to
tipping.

front:
How does the position of the centre of
gravity affect stability?
back:
The position of the centre of gravity
determines whether an object will
remain balanced or topple over when
disturbed.

front:
What happens to an object's centre of
gravity when it is suspended from a
point?
back:
When an object is suspended from a
point, it will settle so that its centre of
gravity comes to rest below the
pivoting point.

front:
True or False?
In an experiment to find the centre of
gravity of an irregular shape, a plumb
line is used to draw a vertical line.
back:
True.
The plumb line is used to draw a vertical
line from the pivot to determine where
the centre of gravity will lie.

front:
How can you locate the centre of gravity
of an irregular shape?
back:
An irregular shape can be suspended
from different points, and a plum line
can be used to draw vertical lines that
intersect at the centre of gravity.

front:
What is the importance of determining
the centre of gravity?
back:
Determining the centre of gravity
enables an understanding of the
stability and balance of an object,
which is crucial in various applications.

True or False?
The centre of gravity of an object is

False.

change depending on the object's

flexible or complex structures.

objects with large momentum.

Momentum can be

conservation of

(Extended Tier

back:
The principle of conservation of momentum states that in a
closed system, the total momentum before an event
equals the total momentum after the event.

front:
True or False?
The conservation
of momentum
applies only to
single objects.
(Extended Tier
Only)
back:
False.
The conservation of momentum applies to systems of
objects, which can include one or multiple objects, as long as
the system is closed.

front:
What is a closed
system in the
context of
momentum?
(Extended Tier
Only)
back:
A closed system in the context of momentum refers to a
system in which the total momentum remains constant, and
no external forces are acting on the system.

front:
State the condition
for momentum to
be conserved in a
collision.
(Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Momentum is conserved in a collision if the system is closed,
meaning there is no net external force acting on it, and
energy within the system remains constant.

True or False?
In the absence of
external forces,
momentum is
always conserved

True.
In the absence of external forces, the momentum of a
collision is a conserved quantity, meaning it remains
constant over time.

Speed is a vector quantity.

Speed is a scalar quantity because it

Average speed is the total distance

Average speed = distance travelled

Velocity describes both magnitude and
direction of motion whereas speed

Velocity is defined as the rate of

Both speed and velocity are measured

velocity values?

The significance of negative velocity

direction.

front:

distance in calculating velocity?

Displacement is different from distance

accounts for direction.

The difference between speed and

velocity is a vector as it includes
direction.

from the average speed?

The total distance is calculated from the
average speed by multiplying the
average speed by the total time taken.

Acceleration is the rate of change of

You can find the change in velocity by

indicate? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
A positive acceleration indicates that
the object is speeding up.

front:
Define acceleration. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Acceleration is the change in an object's
velocity over time.

front:
What does a negative acceleration
indicate? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Negative acceleration indicates that the
object is slowing down.

front:
Define deceleration. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Deceleration is negative acceleration,
it shows an object is slowing down.

front:
What is the acceleration of an object
with constant velocity? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
The acceleration of an object with
constant velocity is zero.

front:
How do you calculate acceleration from
a velocity-time graph? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Acceleration is calculated as the
gradient of a velocity-time graph.

front:
How is direction represented in a
numerical value for acceleration?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The direction of acceleration is
represented by a positive or negative
value.

front:
Which type of graph shows the distance
travelled by a moving object over a
period of time?
back:
A distance-time graph shows the
distance travelled by a moving object
over a period of time.

front:
How is constant speed represented on
a distance-time graph?
back:
On a distance time graph, constant
speed is represented by a straight line:
a steeper slope shows a greater
constant speed
a shallower slope shows a lower
constant speed
a flat, horizontal line shows a
constant speed of zero

front:
How is changing speed represented on
a distance-time graph?
back:
On a distance-time graph, changing
speed is represented by a curved line.

front:
State the equation used to find the
gradient of a distance-time graph.
back:
The equation used to find the gradient
of a distance-time graph is
speed = gradient = ∆ y
∆ x
Where:
∆ y = change in distance
∆ x = change in time

front:
Which line on the distance-time graph
shows the slowest speed?
back:
On a distance-time graph, the line with
the smallest gradient has the slowest
speed. This is the shallowest line (the
orange line).

front:
True or False?
This distance-time graph shows a
stationary object.
back:
True.
A flat, horizontal line on a distance-time
graph shows that the object is
stationary. The distance the object has
travelled is not changing with time.

front:
Describe the motion of the object
shown in this distance-time graph.
back:
The object in this distance-time graph
has an increasing speed. The distance
it travels in each interval of time is
increasing; therefore, the line curves
upward.

front: What does a speed-time graph show?
back:
A speed-time graph shows how the
speed of a moving object varies with
time.

front:
What is constant acceleration on a
speed-time graph?
back:
Constant acceleration on a speed-time
graph is represented by a straight,
sloping line.

front:
True or False?
A gentle slope on a speed-time graph
represents large acceleration.
back:
False.
A gentle slope on a speed-time graph
represents a small acceleration.

front:
Describe the motion shown in this
speed-time graph.
back:
The speed-time graph shows
decreasing acceleration.
The change in speed per unit time
decreases.

front:
What does a flat , horizontal line
represent on a speed-time graph?
back:
A flat, horizontal line indicates that the
acceleration is zero, meaning the
object is moving at a constant speed.

front:
What does the area under a speed-time
graph represent?
back:
The area under a speed-time graph
represents the distance travelled by
the object.

front:
How do you calculate the total area
under a speed-time graph?
back:
The total area under a speed-time
graph shows the total distance
travelled. The total area is the sum of
the areas of each enclosed section
(triangle or rectangle).

front:
What is the formula to calculate the
area of a triangle?
back:
The formula to calculate the area of a
triangle is A = 1 × b × h
Where:
b = base of triangle, measured in
metres (m) or centimetres (cm)
h = height of triangle, measured in
metres (m) or centimetres (cm)

front:
What is the formula to calculate the
area of a rectangle?
back:
The formula to calculate the area of a
rectangle is A = b × h
Where:
b = base of rectangle, measured in
metres (m) or centimetres (cm)
h = height of rectangle, measured
in metres (m) or centimetres (cm)

front:
What shape does the area beneath a
speed-time graph form for an object
with constant speed?
back:
The area under a speed-time graph
forms a rectangle.

front:
True or False?
A flat line on a speed-time graph
indicates constant acceleration.
back:
False.
A flat line on a speed-time graph
indicates constant speed.

front:
True or False?
The starting speed of this object is zero.
back:
False.
The starting speed is not zero because
the line does not start from the origin.

front: Define acceleration of free fall.
back:
Acceleration of free fall is the constant
rate at which all objects fall in the
absence of air resistance, typically
denoted by the symbol g and equal to
approximately 9.81 m/s2 near the
surface of the Earth.

front:
True or False?
All objects fall with the same
acceleration in the presence of air
resistance.
back:
False.
In the presence of air resistance
different objects fall at different
accelerations and not at g. In most
Physics questions we assume that air
resistance is negligible.

front:
What is the value of the constant
acceleration of free fall?
back:
The value of the acceleration of free fall
is g = 9.81m/s2

front:
True or False?
Acceleration of free fall remains
constant regardless of an object's
mass.
back:
True.
Acceleration of free fall remains
constant regardless of an object's mass.

front:
Define terminal velocity. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Terminal velocity is the constant speed
reached by a falling object when the
upward force of drag equals the
downward force of weight, resulting in
zero acceleration.

front: What is the equation for weight?
back:
The equation for weight is W = mg
Where:
W = weight measured in newtons
(N)
m = mass measured in kilograms
(kg)
g = acceleration of freefall (m/s2)

front: Define air resistance.
back:
Air resistance is the frictional force
exerted by air particles on objects
moving through air, which opposes the
direction of motion.

front:
How does air resistance affect the
motion of falling objects? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Air resistance opposes the motion of
objects falling through air, exerting an
upward force that increases with the
object's speed.

front:
True or False?
Air resistance decreases as the speed of
a falling object increases. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
False.
Air resistance increases as the speed of
a falling object increases.

front:
What is the relationship between the
forces of weight and air resistance
during free fall? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
During free fall, weight acts
downwards while air resistance acts
upwards. As the speed of the object
increases, air resistance increases until
it equals the weight and terminal
velocity is reached.

front:
How does terminal velocity affect the
acceleration of a falling object?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Terminal velocity occurs when the
acceleration of a falling object
becomes zero because the upward drag
force equals the downward force of
weight, resulting in a constant speed.

front:
True or False?
Air resistance remains constant during
the fall of a skydiver. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
False.
The air resistance changes with speed
during the fall of a skydiver.

front:
What factors affect the acceleration of
freefall? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The acceleration of free fall is affected
by the gravitational field strength . It
is independent of the mass of the falling
object.

front: Define weight.
back:
Weight is the gravitational force exerted
on an object with mass.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front: What is a ruler?
back:
A ruler is a device used to measure
small distances of a few centimetres.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
True or False?
Rulers measure to the nearest
millimetre.
back:
True.
Rulers measure to the nearest
millimetre.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front: What is the purpose of a tape measure?
back:
A tape measure is appropriate for
measuring distances of a few metres.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
Which device can be used to measure
distances of up to a kilometre?
back:
A trundle wheel is used to measure
large distances up to a kilometre.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front: What is a measuring cylinder?
back:
A measuring cylinder is a device used to
measure the volume of liquids.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
What device can be used to measure
time intervals?
back:
A stopwatch can be used to measure
time intervals.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front: Define the term reaction time.
back:
Reaction time is how long it takes
someone to react to an event.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
True or False?
Human reaction time has more of an
impact on short-time measurements
than long-time measurements.
back:
True.
Human reaction time has more of an
impact on short-time measurements
than long-time measurements.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
State the equation for calculating an
average.
back:
The equation for calculating an average
is average = total value
number of values

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
What is the purpose of taking multiple
readings in Physics?
back:
The purpose of taking multiple readings
in Physics is to obtain an accurate
measurement value.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
Define a scalar quantity. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
A scalar quantity is a quantity that has
only magnitude.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
What is a vector quantity? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
A vector quantity is a quantity that has
both magnitude and direction.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
What is displacement? (Extended Tier
Only)
back: The distance from a starting point.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
True or False?
Mass is a scalar quantity. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
True.
Mass is a scalar quantity as it has only
magnitude.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
True or False?
Distance is a scalar quantity. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
True.
Distance is a scalar quantity.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
How can you determine whether a
quantity is a scalar or vector?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Determine if it has only magnitude
(scalar) or magnitude and direction
(vector).

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
Is 100 km due north a scalar or a vector
quantity? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
100 km due north is a vector quantity
because it includes both a magnitude
and a direction.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
True or False?
Energy is a scalar. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True
Energy is a scalar.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
Is temperature a scalar or a vector?
(Extended Tier Only)
back: Temperature is a scalar.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
Is electric field strength a scalar or a
vector? (Extended Tier Only)
back: Electric field strength is a vector.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
How are vectors represented?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Vectors are represented by an arrow
where the arrowhead indicates
direction and the length represents
magnitude.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
Define component vectors. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Component vectors are parts of a
vector that act in specific directions ,
often indicated by subscripts.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
State the equation to calculate the
resultant vector using Pythagoras'
Theorem. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
c 2 = b 2 + a 2
Where:
c = longest side length of a right-
angled triangle, measured
depending on the quantity it
represents
b = one of the side lengths of a
right-angled triangle, measured
depending on the quantity it
represents
a = the other side length of a right
angles triangle, measured
depending on the quantity it
represents

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
What is the SOH-CAH-TOA mnemonic
used for in trigonometry? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
The SOH-CAH-TOA mnemonic in
trigonometry is used to remember how
to apply sine and cosine to resolve the
sides of a triangle when calculating
vectors.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
How can you find the angle of the
resultant vector? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Trigonometry can be used to find the
angle of the resultant vector.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
How can vectors be calculated
graphically? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Vectors can be calculated graphically by
carefully producing a scale drawing
with all lengths and angles correct using
a pencil, ruler and protractor.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
Which theorem is essential for
calculating the magnitude of vectors at
right angles to each other? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Pythagoras' theorem is essential for
calculating the magnitude of vectors at
right angles to each other.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
Define resultant vector. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
A resultant vector is a single vector
with the same effect as two or more
vectors combined.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
True or False?
The graphical calculation method of
resolving vectors requires an exact
scale. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
The graphical method doesn't require
an exact scale.

subtopicFull: T1.8 — physical quantities and measurement techniques
front:
What does the length of the vector
arrow represent? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The length of the arrow represents the
magnitude of the vector.

front: What is pressure?
back:
Pressure is defined as the concentration
of a force or the force per unit area.

front:
State the equation relating pressure,
force and area.
back:
The equation for pressure, force and
area is P = F
A
Where:
P = pressure, measured in pascals
(Pa)
F = force, measured in newton's (N)
A = surface area, measured in
metres squared (m2)

front:
True or False?
Pressure is measured in pascals (Pa).
back:
True.
Pressure is measured in pascals (Pa).

front:
What is the relationship between
force, pressure and surface area?
back:
A force applied over a large area will
result in a small pressure, and vice
versa.

front:
True or False?
A high-heeled shoe produces the same
pressure on the ground as a flat-soled
shoe when worn by the same person.
back:
False.
A high-heeled shoe produces a higher
pressure on the ground than a flat-
soled shoe when worn by the same
person.
This is because the same force is
applied over a smaller surface area.

front: Why do tractors need large tyres?
back:
Tractors need large tyres to spread their
weight over a large area to reduce the
pressure they exert on the ground.
This prevents them from sinking into
the mud.

front:
What happens when a force is applied
to a nail placed against a wall?
back:
When a force is applied to the nail, it
pierces and enters the wall.
This is because the applied force is
concentrated at the sharp pointed end,
which produces a large pressure over a
small area.

front:
True or False?
The area used in calculating the
pressure should always be the cross-
sectional area of the object.
back:
True.
The area used in calculating the
pressure should always be the cross-
sectional area of the object.
This is the area which is perpendicular
(90 degrees) to the applied force.

front:
A box is placed on a table. Calculate the
pressure applied by the grey face of the
box onto the table.
back:
The pressure applied by the grey face of
the box onto the table is 4 Pa.

front: Define a fluid .
back: A fluid is either a liquid or a gas.

front:
How does a liquid exert force on an
object suspended in it?
back:
When an object is suspended in a liquid,
it exerts pressure evenly across the
whole surface of the object and in all
directions.
This pressure creates a force which acts
at 90 degrees (right angles) to each
surface.

front:
How does increasing depth and
density affect the pressure of a liquid?
back:
The pressure of a liquid increases with
both increased depth and increased
density of the liquid.

front:
True or False?
The force created by pressure in a liquid
is exerted on an object in one direction
only.
back:
False.
The force created by pressure in a liquid
is exerted evenly across the whole
surface of an object.

front:
State the equation for the pressure
difference of an object in a fluid.
back:
The equation for pressure difference in
a fluid is ∆ p = ρg ∆ h
Where:
∆ p = change in pressure,
measured in pascals (Pa)
ρ = density of the liquid, measured
in kilograms per metre cubed
(kg/m3)
g = gravitational field strength on
Earth, measured in newtons per
kilogram (N/kg)
∆ h = change in depth of the object
in the liquid, measured in metres
(m)

front:
State the meaning of ∆ p in equation
∆ p = ρg ∆ h . (Extended Tier Only)
back:
In the pressure equation for liquids ∆ p
represents the change in pressure in
pascals (Pa).

front:
State the meaning of ρ in the equation
∆ p = ρg ∆ h . (Extended Tier Only)
back:
ρ in the pressure equation for liquids
stands for the density of the liquid,
measured in kilograms per metre cubed
(kg/m3).

front:
What quantities are needed to calculate
the depth of water in a swimming pool?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The depth of water in a swimming pool
can be calculated using the pressure
equation: ∆ p = ρg ∆ h
The quantities needed to calculate
depth ∆ h are:
∆ p = the pressure of the water at
the bottom of the pool
ρ = the density of the water
g = the gravitational field strength
of Earth

front:
State the property of pressure in a
liquid demonstrated in the diagram.
back:
The property of pressure in a liquid
demonstrated in the diagram is that
pressure increases with depth.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
What are the three different states of
matter?
back:
The three states of matter are:
solid
liquid
gas

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
Solids are not compressible.
back:
True.
Solids (and liquids) are not
compressible.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
Liquids have a definite shape.
back:
False.
Solids have a definite shape. Liquids
take the shape of their container.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
Which state of matter has no definite
shape and a fixed volume?
back:
Liquids have no definite shape and a
fixed volume.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
Gases have a definite volume.
back:
False.
Solids have a definite volume. Gases
have no fixed volume.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front: Which state of matter is compressible?
back:
Gases are the only state of matter that
is compressible.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front: What are the properties of a solid?
back:
The properties of a solid are:
definite shape
definite volume
cannot flow
not compressible

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front: What are the properties of a liquid?
back:
The properties of a liquid are:
no definite shape
fixed volume
can flow
not compressible

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front: What are the properties of a gas?
back:
The properties of a gas are:
no definite shape
no fixed volume
can flow
are compressible

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
Identify the particle arrangement that
represents a solid.
back:
The first particle arrangement
represents a solid.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
Identify the particle arrangement that
represents a gas.
back:
The third particle arrangement
represents a gas.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
In which state of matter do the particles
vibrate about their fixed positions?
back:
The particles in solids vibrate about
their fixed positions

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
The particles are closer together in a
gas than in a liquid.
back:
False.
The particles in a gas are further apart
than the particles in a liquid.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
In which state of matter are the
particles free to slide past one another?
back:
The particles in a liquid are free to slide
past one another?

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
In which state of matter are the
particles widely separated?
back:
The particles in a gas are widely
separated.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
In which states of matter are the
particles randomly arranged?
back:
The particles in gases and liquids are
randomly arranged.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
The particles in a liquid are arranged in
a regular pattern.
back:
False.
The particles in a solid are arranged in a
regular pattern. The particles in a liquid
are randomly arranged.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
In which state of matter do particles
have the most energy? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
The particles in a gas have the most
energy. They are energetic enough to
have overcome the intermolecular
forces of attraction.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
The particles in which state of matter
have the least energy? (Extended Tier
Only) to overcome the intermolecular forces
back:
The particles in a solid have the least
energy. They are not energetic enough
holding them together.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
In which state of matter do particles
have enough energy to partially
overcome the intermolecular forces of
attraction? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The particles in a liquid have enough
energy to partially overcome the
intermolecular forces of attraction. They
have enough energy to slide over one
another, but not enough to completely
overcome the forces holding them
together.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
The amount of pressure that a gas
exerts on its container is dependent on
the temperature of the gas.
back:
True.
The pressure exerted by a gas on its
container is dependent on the
temperature because the particles gain
energy in their kinetic store as they are
heated.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front: Define absolute zero.
back:
Absolute zero is the lowest temperature
possible. At zero degrees kelvin (K) the
particles would not be moving, and
therefore would not exert any pressure.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
What temperature is absolute zero in
degrees Celsius?
back: Absolute zero is –273 °C (which is 0 K).

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
The particles in a gas are in constant
random motion at high speeds.
back:
True.
The particles in a gas are in constant
random motion at high speeds.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
Gases moving in random thermal
motion collide with the surfaces of the
container and with other gas particles.
back:
True.
Gases moving in random thermal
motion collide with the surfaces of the
container and with other gas particles.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
What causes the pressure in a gas when
it is contained?
back:
Pressure in a gas is caused by collisions
of the gas particles with the walls of the
container.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front: State the equation for pressure.
back:
The equation for pressure due to
contact between two surfaces is P = F
A
Where:
P = pressure, measured in pascals
(Pa)
F = force, measured in newtons (N)
A = area, measured in metres
squared (m2)

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front: Define pressure. (Extended Tier Only)
back: Pressure is force per unit area.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
Define gas pressure in terms of force.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Gas pressure is the force exerted by the
gas particles colliding with surfaces per
unit area.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front: Define Brownian motion.
back:
Brownian motion is the random
movement of larger particles in a liquid
or gas produced by large numbers of
collisions with smaller particles.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
Brownian motion is evidence
supporting the Big Bang theory.
back:
False.
Brownian motion is evidence
supporting the kinetic theory of
matter.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
Brownian motion explains the random
thermal motion of particles suspended
in liquids and gases.
back:
True.
Brownian motion explains the random
thermal motion of particles suspended
in liquids and gases.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
When small particles such as pollen or
smoke are suspended in a liquid or gas,
they can be microscopically observed to
be moving erratically. What is causing
them to move?
back:
When small particles such as pollen or
smoke are suspended in a liquid or gas,
they can be microscopically observed to
be moving erratically. This is because
they collide with smaller atoms and
molecules in the air or water.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
When observing Brownian motion, the
water or air particles in the suspension
can be seen under a microscope.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Water molecules, and the atoms and
molecules in air, are too small to be
seen under a microscope. It is because
they cannot be seen when observing
Brownian motion that the smoke or
pollen particles appear to be moving
erratically.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
When observing pollen suspended in
air, what causes the Brownian motion?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The atoms and molecules in the air
collide with the pollen particles. The
atoms and molecules are too small to
be seen by the microscope, so the
pollen particles appear to be moving
erratically.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
It is possible to have negative values of
temperature in degrees kelvin.
back:
False.
It is not possible to have negative
values of temperature in degrees kelvin.
0 K is absolute zero, the lowest possible
temperature.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
10 °C = 283 K
back:
True.
0 °C = 273 K, and an increase of 1 °C is
equal to an increase in 1 K. Therefore,
10 °C = 283 K

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
If the temperature of a gas remains
constant, what happens to the pressure
when the volume is decreased?
back:
If the temperature of a gas remains
constant, the pressure increases when
the volume is decreased.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
If the temperature of a gas in a balloon
remains constant, what happens to the
volume when the pressure is
decreased?
back:
If the temperature of a gas in a balloon
remains constant, the volume
increases when the pressure is
decreased.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
If the volume of a gas remains constant,
what happens to the pressure when the
temperature is increased?
back:
If the volume of a gas remains constant,
the pressure increases when the
temperature is increased.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
The hotter the gas, the more energy the
gas particles have in their kinetic store.
back:
True.
The hotter the gas, the more energy the
gas particles have in their kinetic store.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
True or False?
The cooler a gas is, the faster the gas
particles move around.
back:
False.
The cooler a gas is, the slower the gas
particles move around, because they
have less energy in their kinetic store.

subtopicFull: T2.1 — Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
front:
Define Boyle's law. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Boyle's law states that the pressure of a
gas at a constant temperature is
inversely proportional to its volume.

front: Define thermal expansion.
back:
Thermal expansion occurs when
substances are heated due to the
increased movement of the particles in
the substance.

front:
True or False?
When materials are heated they
contract.
back:
False.
When materials are heated they
expand.

front:
True or False?
In thermal expansion, the size of the
particles increases.
back:
False.
The particles themselves do not
expand. The particles gain energy when
heated, so they move around faster
which causes the space between
particles to increase. This leads to the
overall expansion of the substance.

front:
When the temperature is increased
which substance expands the most?
back:
When the temperature is increased a
gas expands the most.

front:
True or False?
In thermal expansion, solids expand
more than gases. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
In thermal expansion, gases expand the
most, then liquids, and solids expand
the least.

front:
Name two applications of thermal
expansion.
back:
The two applications of thermal
expansion that you need to know are:
thermometers
temperature activated switches

front:
True or False?
Railway tracks and bridges have gaps
built in to accommodate thermal
expansion.
back:
True.
Railway tracks and bridges do have gaps
built in to allow for the thermal
expansion of the materials.

front: Define the term internal energy.
back:
Internal energy is the total energy of the
particles in a system due to their motion
and position.

front:
True or False?
The change in temperature of a
substance that is heated depends on
the mass of the substance.
back:
True.
The change in temperature of a
substance that is heated does depend
on the mass of the substance.

front:
What does the temperature increase
of a system depend upon?
back:
The temperature increase of a system
depends upon:
The mass of the substance heated
The type of material
The amount of thermal energy
transferred to the system

front: Define the term specific heat capacity.
back:
The specific heat capacity of a
substance is the amount of energy
required to raise the temperature of 1
kg of the substance by 1 °C.

front:
True or False?
A substance with a low specific heat
capacity will heat up and cool down
slowly.
back:
False.
A substance with a low specific heat
capacity will heat up and cool down
quickly. It takes less energy to create a
temperature change.

front:
True or False?
Different substances have different
specific heat capacities.
back:
True.
Different substances have different
specific heat capacities.

State the equation for specific heat
capacity. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The equation for specific heat capacity
is ∆ E = mc ∆ θ

What is the equation for specific heat

back:
