front:
What are the melting and boiling points
of pure water at standard atmospheric
pressure?
back:
Pure water ice melts at 0 °C, and pure
liquid water boils at 100 °C at standard
atmospheric pressure. These are known
as the fixed points of water.

front:
True or False?
Energy is transferred away from a
substance when it solidifies.
back:
True.
Energy is transferred away from a
substance when it solidifies.

front:
True or False?
The temperature of a substance
increases while the substance is
melting.
back:
False.
The temperature of a substance does
not increase while the substance is
melting. There is no change in
temperature during a change of state.
The energy is used to change the state
of the substance rather than to increase
its temperature.

front:
True or False?
Liquids freeze at the melting point of
the substance.
back:
True.
Liquids do freeze at the melting point of
the substance. The state change
between solids and liquids occurs at the
melting point.

front:
True or False?
Gases condense at the boiling point of
the substance.
back:
True.
Gases do condense at the boiling point
of the substance. The state change
between liquids and gases occurs at the
boiling point of the substance.

front:
When a substance is melting or boiling,
why does the temperature of the
substance not change even though
energy is being transferred into the
system? proximity, rather than increasing the
back:
The energy transferred into a substance
that is melting or boiling is used to
overcome the intermolecular forces of
attraction holding the particles in close
temperature of the substance.

front:
True or False?
Freezing and melting happen at the
same temperature.
back:
True.
Freezing and melting do happen at the
same temperature, the melting point of
the substance.

front: Define the term evaporation.
back:
Evaporation is the change of state from
a liquid to a gas. It happens at any
temperature and only from the surface
of the liquid.

front:
True or False?
Evaporation results in the heating of a
liquid.
back:
False.
Evaporation results in the cooling of a
liquid.

front: How does evaporation occur?
back:
Evaporation occurs when more
energetic particles at the surface of
the liquid overcome the intermolecular
forces of attraction holding them in
close proximity.

front:
What are the three steps in the cooling
effect of evaporation?
back:
Evaporation cools a substance because:
The more energetic particles at the
surface escape the liquid.
This reduces the average energy
of the particles in the liquid.
Since temperature is a measure of
the average kinetic energy of the
particles in a substance, the
temperature decreases and the
substance is cooled.

front:
What are the factors affecting the rate
of evaporation? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The factors affecting the rate of
evaporation are:
temperature
surface area
air movement

front:
What is the difference between boiling
and evaporation? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Boiling only happens at the boiling
point of a substance, and it occurs
throughout the liquid. Evaporation
can occur at any temperature and it
only happens at the surface of a liquid.

front:
True or False?
Objects can be cooled when a liquid
evaporates from the surface of an
object. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
Objects can be cooled when a liquid
evaporates from the surface of an
object. For example, when sweat
evaporates from the skin:
Energy is transferred from the
warmer skin to the cooler liquid.
The more energetic particles at the
surface of the liquid escape
reducing the average energy of the
liquid.
This increases the temperature
difference between the skin and
the liquid so more energy is
transferred from the skin to the
liquid.
This process has a cooling effect
on the skin.

front:
Define thermal conduction.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Thermal conduction is the transfer of
thermal energy through a substance.

front:
True or False?
Thermal conduction in solids occurs
when hotter, more energetic atoms or
ions vibrate faster and collide with
neighbouring atoms or ions. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
True.
Thermal conduction in solids occurs
when hotter, more energetic atoms or
ions vibrate faster and collide with
neighbouring atoms or ions,
transferring energy throughout the
structure of the solid.

front:
Why does thermal conduction generally
occur faster in metals than non-metals?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Thermal conduction occurs faster in
metals because metals have free
(delocalised) electrons, which speed up
the energy transfer throughout the
substance.

front:
When does thermal conduction end?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Thermal conduction ends when thermal
equilibrium is reached.

front:
Define thermal equilibrium.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Thermal equilibrium is a state in which
no net energy transfer takes place
because a consistent temperature has
been reached.

front:
True or False?
Thermal conduction does not happen in
liquids or gases because the particles
are too far apart. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Thermal conduction does happen in
liquids and gases, but they tend to be
poor conductors because the particles
are further apart than in solids.

front:
True or False?
Convection cannot happen in solids.
back:
True.
Convection only happens in liquids and
gases because the particles are free to
move around. It cannot happen in
solids because the particles are held in
a rigid structure.

front:
How is a convection current set up
when a fluid is heated?
back:
When a fluid is heated, the space
between particles increases, so the
density of the fluid decreases which
causes it to rise, and cooler, denser fluid
takes its place.

front:
In a convection current hot fluid
expands and rises. What is this
replaced by?
back:
In a convection current hot fluid
expands and rises. In a convection
current, this is replaced by cooler,
denser fluid.

front:
What substance is used as a purple dye
to demonstrate convection in water?
back:
Potassium permanganate is used as a
purple dye to demonstrate convection
in water.

front:
True or False?
Heat rises.
back:
False.
Heat is not a substance so it cannot rise.
It is the heated region of the fluid that
rises as its density decreases.

front:
True or False?
Convection currents form when a fluid
is cooled.
back:
True.
When a fluid is cooled, the movement of
the particles slows down and they come
closer together increasing the density.
The denser fluid sinks and less dense
fluid takes its place.

front:
True or False?
All objects emit thermal radiation.
back:
True.
All objects emit thermal radiation. The
hotter an object is, the more thermal
radiation it emits.

front:
True or False?
The colour of an object affects its ability
to emit and absorb radiation.
back:
True.
The colour of an object does affect its
ability to emit and absorb thermal
radiation.

front:
True or False?
Thermal radiation requires a medium to
travel through.
back:
False.
Thermal radiation is an
electromagnetic wave, so it can travel
through a vacuum.

front:
What type of electromagnetic wave is
thermal radiation?
back: Thermal radiation is infrared radiation.

front:
In terms of the rate of energy transfer,
how does an object maintain a constant
temperature? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
An object maintains a constant
temperature when the rate of energy
transfer away from the object is equal
to the rate of energy transfer to the
object.

front:
True or False?
White surfaces are good emitters and
good absorbers of thermal radiation.
back:
False.
White surfaces are poor emitters and
poor absorbers of thermal radiation.

front:
True or False?
When an object emits less thermal
radiation than it absorbs, its
temperature increases. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
When an object emits less thermal
radiation than it absorbs, its
temperature increases.

front:
What colour surface is the best emitter
of thermal radiation?
back:
Black surfaces are the best emitters of
thermal radiation.

front:
True or False?
Shiny surfaces are very good emitters of
thermal radiation.
back:
False.
Shiny surfaces are very poor emitters of
thermal radiation. They are also very
poor absorbers because they reflect the
infrared radiation.

front:
True or False?
When an object emits more thermal
radiation than it absorbs, its
temperature increases. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
False.
When an object emits more thermal
radiation than it absorbs, its
temperature decreases.

front:
True or False?
If the Earth had no atmosphere, the
temperature on the surface would
remain the same as it is currently.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
If the Earth had no atmosphere, the
temperature on the surface would drop
to about −180 °C at night, the same as
that of the Moon at night.

front:
Define the Greenhouse Effect .
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The Greenhouse Effect is the process by
which certain gases in the Earth's
atmosphere trap and reradiate infrared
radiation, leading to an increase in the
temperature of the Earth's surface.

front:
What are the factors affecting the
Earth's temperature? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
The factors affecting the Earth's
temperature are the rate of reflection ,
absorption, and emission of light and
infrared radiation from the Sun.

front:
True or False?
The Earth receives thermal radiation
from the Sun but does not emit its own
thermal radiation. (Extended Tier
Only) emit thermal radiation.
back:
False.
The Earth receives thermal radiation
from the Sun and emits its own thermal
radiation. Remember that all objects

front:
Define Greenhouse Gases. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Greenhouse gases are gases in the
atmosphere that absorb and reradiate
longer-wavelength infrared radiation
emitted by the Earth, preventing it from
escaping into space, and causing
warming of the Earth's surface.

front:
How does the Greenhouse Effect cause
warming of the Earth's surface?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The Greenhouse Effect causes warming
of the Earth's surface because of the
Sun's thermal radiation reaching the
Earth's atmosphere. Here some
radiation is reflected back into space,
and the rest is absorbed and reradiated
by greenhouse gases, warming the
atmosphere and Earth's surface.

front:
What is an example of a greenhouse
gas? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Examples of greenhouse gases are:
carbon dioxide
methane (natural gas)
water vapour

front:
True or False?
The electromagnetic spectrum is
arranged in a specific order based on
the wavelengths or frequencies.
back:
True.
The electromagnetic spectrum is
arranged in a specific order based on
the wavelengths or frequencies.

front:
What is the order of the
electromagnetic spectrum from longest
to shortest wavelength?
back:
The order of the electromagnetic
spectrum from longest to shortest
wavelength is:
Radio waves
Microwaves
Infrared
Visible light
Ultraviolet
X-rays
Gamma rays

front:
What are the properties of
electromagnetic waves?
back:
All electromagnetic waves share the
following properties:
transverse
can through a vacuum
travel at the same speed in a
vacuum
form a continuous spectrum

front:
Define the term electromagnetic
waves.
back:
Electromagnetic waves are transverse
waves with oscillating electric and
magnetic fields that transfer energy
from the source of the waves to an
absorber.

front:
True or False?
The speed of electromagnetic waves in
air is the same as in a vacuum.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
The speed of electromagnetic waves in
air can be approximated to the speed of
light in a vacuum because the
difference in speed is so small.

front:
What is the relationship between the
frequency of electromagnetic waves
and the energy they transfer?
back:
The higher the frequency, the higher
the energy of the radiation, and vice
versa.

front:
What is a mnemonic for remembering
the order of radiation types in the
electromagnetic spectrum?
back:
One possible mnemonic for
remembering the electromagnetic
spectrum is:
Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using
X-ray Guns.

front:
Identify using the diagram the
electromagnetic radiation type with the
shortest wavelength.
back:
The electromagnetic radiation type with
the shortest wavelength is gamma
rays.

front:
Identify using the diagram the
electromagnetic radiation type with the
highest frequency.
back:
The electromagnetic radiation type with
the highest frequency is gamma rays.

front: Define the term fluorescence .
back:
Fluorescence is the process where
certain substances absorb ultraviolet
light and re-emit it as visible light,
causing them to glow.

front:
What is the main application of radio
waves?
back:
The main application of radio waves is
in wireless communications.

front:
What are the two main applications of
microwaves?
back:
The two main applications of
microwaves are:
heating food
wireless communications

front:
True or False?
Night vision cameras use infrared
radiation.
back:
True.
One application of infrared radiation is
night vision cameras.

front:
True or False?
Gamma radiation is used in fibre optic
communications.
back:
False.
Infrared and visible light are used in
optic fibre communications. Gamma
rays are used for sterilising medical
equipment and treating cancer.

front:
True or False?
Sterilising water and detecting fake
bank notes are two applications of X-
rays.
back:
False.
Sterilising water and detecting fake
bank notes are two applications of
ultraviolet radiation (UV). X-rays are
used for imaging in medicine, dentistry,
airport security and industry.

front:
True or False?
Visible light is the only part of the
electromagnetic spectrum that human
eyes can see.
back:
True.
Human eyes can only detect
wavelengths of electromagnetic
radiation in the visible light section of
the electromagnetic spectrum.

front:
True or False?
Remote controls are one application of
ultraviolet radiation.
back:
False.
Ultraviolet radiation carries too much
energy and would be harmful if used for
this purpose. Remote controls are one
application of infrared radiation.

front:
State the type of radiation used in the
device in the diagram.
back:
The device in the diagram is a
microwave oven and uses microwaves.

front:
True or False?
As the frequency of electromagnetic
waves increases, so does the energy
and the danger associated with them.
back:
True.
As the frequency of electromagnetic
waves increases, the energy they
transfer increases, and therefore so
does the danger associated with them.

front:
What is the main danger associated
with ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma
rays?
back:
Ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays can
all ionise atoms, which can damage
cells and cause mutations, which can
lead to cancer.

front:
True or False?
Radio waves are known to be harmful
to humans.
back:
False.
There are no known harmful effects of
radio waves.

front:
True or False?
Microwaves can be harmful to humans.
back:
True.
Microwaves can be harmful to humans
in high levels of exposure, because
higher-frequency microwaves cause
internal heating.

front:
True or False?
Mobile phones emit microwave
radiation.
back:
True.
Mobile phones do emit microwave
radiation, but only at low energies
which are not known to cause any
harm.

front:
True or False?
Ultraviolet radiation can be harmful to
humans.
back:
True.
Ultraviolet radiation can cause sunburn,
eye damage and skin cancer.

front:
True or False?
X-rays and gamma rays can be harmful
to humans.
back:
True.
X-rays and gamma rays (and UV) are
ionising radiation which can remove
electrons from atoms, causing damage
to DNA which can lead to cell and tissue
damage, mutations and cancer.

front:
True or False?
Sunscreen absorbs ultraviolet light,
preventing it from damaging the skin.
back:
True.
Sunscreen absorbs ultraviolet light,
preventing it from damaging the skin.

front:
True or False?
Ionising forms of electromagnetic
radiation have a higher frequency than
visible light.
back:
True.
The ionising forms of electromagnetic
radiation are ultraviolet, X-rays and
gamma rays, all of which have higher
frequencies than visible light.

front:
True or False?
The longer the wavelength, the more
ionising the electromagnetic radiation.
back:
False.
The shorter the wavelength (and
therefore, the higher the frequency),
the more ionising the electromagnetic
radiation.

front:
State the purpose of the device in the
image.
back:
The device in the image is a radiation
badge and its purpose is to measure a
person's exposure to radiation.

front: What is a geostationary satellite?
back:
A geostationary satellite is a satellite
that orbits above the Earth's equator.

front:
What is the orbital period of a
geostationary satellite?
back:
The orbital period of a geostationary
satellite is 24 hours.

front:
True or False?
Polar satellites orbit higher above the
Earth's surface than geostationary
satellites.
back:
False.
Geostationary satellites orbit much
higher above the Earth's surface than
polar satellites do.

front:
What are geostationary satellites used
for?
back:
The high orbit of geostationary satellites
makes them useful for radio and
telecommunications broadcasting
around the world.

front: What is a polar satellite?
back:
A polar satellite is a satellite that orbits
around the Earth's north and south
poles.

front:
True or False?
Polar satellites are also known as low-
orbit satellites.
back:
True.
Polar satellites are also known as low-
orbit satellites because they orbit much
closer to the Earth's surface than
geostationary satellites.

front: What are polar satellites used for?
back:
Polar satellites are used for:
monitoring the weather
military applications
taking images of the Earth's surface

front:
Why are polar satellites used for
military applications rather than
geostationary satellites?
back:
Polar satellites have a lower orbit,
therefore there is a much shorter time
delay between sending and receiving
signals, and the images are much
clearer. This makes polar satellites more
suitable for certain applications
including military use.

front:
Why are microwaves used for wireless
internet? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Microwaves are used for wireless
internet (WiFi) because microwaves can
penetrate some walls and only require a
short ariel for transmission and
reception.

front:
Why are radio waves used for
Bluetooth? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Radio waves can pass through walls but
the signal is weakened by doing so,
therefore radio waves are useful for
very short-range communications such
as Bluetooth.

front:
True or False?
The value of an analogue signal can
vary continuously. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
The value of analogue signals can vary
continuously. They can take any value.

front:
What type of signal can only take one of
two discrete states? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Digital signals can only take discrete
states such as:
1 and 0
high and low
on and off

front:
True or False?
One advantage of a digital signal over
an analogue signal is that a digital signal
can be regenerated so there is minimal
noise. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
A digital signal can be regenerated
(restored to its original characteristics)
so there is minimal noise (unwanted
disturbance in the signal). This increases
the range of the signal so it can be
transmitted over larger distances.

front: Define the term amplitude.
back:
Amplitude is the distance from the
undisturbed position to the peak or
trough of a wave.

front: What is wavelength?
back:
Wavelength is the distance from one
point on the wave to the same point on
the next wave.

front: Define the term frequency.
back:
Frequency is the number of waves
passing a point in a second.

front: Define the term wave speed.
back:
Wave speed is the speed at which a
wave travels.

front: What is a wavefront?
back:
A wavefront is a way of picturing waves
as if from above, where each wavefront
represents the peak of a single wave.

front: What is a ripple tank used for?
back:
A ripple tank is used to demonstrate
wave motion.

front: What is the symbol used for amplitude?
back: The symbol used for amplitude is A .

front: What are the units of amplitude?
back: The units of amplitude are metres (m).

Identify the wave property indicated by
the arrow on the diagram.
back:
The wave property indicated by the

front: What are the units of wave speed?
back:
The units of wave speed are metres per
second (m/s).

front: What is the symbol for wave speed?
back: The symbol for wave speed is v .

front:
True or False?
The symbol for frequency is λ .
back:
False.
The symbol for frequency is f .

front:
True or False?
The units of frequency are hertz (Hz).
back:
True.
The units of frequency are hertz (Hz)

front: What are the units for wavelength?
back:
The units for wavelength are metres
(m).

front: What is the symbol for wavelength?
back: The symbol for wavelength is λ .

State the wave equation in terms of
wave speed.

The wave equation in terms of wave

front: Define the term transverse wave.
back:
A transverse wave is a wave where the
oscillations are at right angles
(perpendicular) to the direction of
energy transfer.

front:
What are three examples of transverse
waves?
back:
Examples of transverse waves include:
ripples on the surface of water
vibrations on a guitar string
S-waves (secondary seismic waves)
electromagnetic waves

front: Define the term longitudinal wave.
back:
A longitudinal wave is a wave where the
oscillations are parallel to the direction
of energy transfer.

front:
What are three examples of longitudinal
waves?
back:
Examples of longitudinal waves are:
sound waves
P-waves (primary seismic waves)
pressure waves in liquids or gases

front:
True or False?
Longitudinal waves can travel in a
vacuum.
back:
False.
Longitudinal waves require a medium
to travel through, so they cannot travel
in a vacuum since there are no particles
in a vacuum.

front:
What is the name for the part of a
longitudinal wave where the particles
are close together?
back:
In a longitudinal wave, the area where
the particles are close together is called
a compression.

front:
What is the name for the part of a
longitudinal wave where the particles
are spaced far apart?
back:
In a longitudinal wave, the area where
the particles are spaced far apart is
called a rarefaction.

front:
True or False?
Visible light is an example of a
transverse wave.
back:
True.
Visible light is part of the
electromagnetic spectrum. All
electromagnetic waves are transverse
waves.

front:
True or False?
Transverse waves can travel through a
vacuum.
back:
True.
Electromagnetic waves are transverse
waves and they can travel through a
vacuum. However, other types of
transverse waves such as water waves
and S-waves are mechanical waves that
require a medium.

front:
What is the key difference between
transverse and longitudinal waves?
back:
The key difference between transverse
and longitudinal waves is the direction
of the vibrations with respect to the
direction of the energy transfer. For
transverse waves, the vibrations are
perpendicular to the direction of energy
transfer, while for longitudinal waves,
the vibrations are parallel to the
direction of energy transfer.

front:
True or False?
The highest point above the rest
position of a transverse wave is called
the peak of the wave.
back:
True.
The highest point above the rest
position of a transverse wave is called
the peak or the crest of the wave.

front: Define the term reflection .
back:
Reflection occurs when a wave meets a
boundary between two media and does
not pass through, but instead stays in
the original medium.

front: State the law of reflection .
back:
The law of reflection states that the
angle of incidence is equal to the angle
of reflection.

front: Define the term refraction.
back:
Refraction occurs when a wave passes a
boundary between two different
transparent media and undergoes a
change in speed causing it to change
direction.

front: Define the term diffraction .
back:
Diffraction is when waves pass around
an obstacle or through a narrow gap,
and the waves spread out.

front:
True or False?
Diffraction only happens when the gap
the wave is passing through is smaller
than the wavelength of the wave.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Diffraction is greatest when the gap the
wave is passing through is of a similar
size to the wavelength of the wave. If
the wavelength is much greater than, or
much smaller than the gap then no
diffraction will occur.

front:
True or False?
The angle of incidence is measured
between the incident ray and the
boundary surface.
back:
False.
The angle of incidence is measured
between the incident ray and the
normal.

front:
True or False?
The angle of reflection is measured
between the incident ray and the
normal.
back:
False.
The angle of reflection is measured
between the reflected ray and the
normal.

front:
What is the key difference between
reflection and refraction?
back:
Reflection is when a wave stays in the
same medium, while refraction is when
a wave passes into a different medium
and changes speed.

front:
True or False?
The angle of incidence is equal to the
angle of refraction.
back:
False.
The law of reflection states that the
angle of incidence is equal to the angle
of reflection . In refraction, the angle
of refraction is dependent upon the
angle of incidence and the media
through which the wave travels.

front:
How do you measure the angle of
refraction?
back:
The angle of refraction is measured with
a protractor between the refracted ray
and the normal.

front:
What types of wave behaviour can a
ripple tank be used to demonstrate?
back:
A ripple tank can be used to
demonstrate the following types of
wave behaviour:
reflection
refraction
diffraction

front:
True or False?
The amount of diffraction depends on
the size of the gap compared to the
wavelength. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
The amount of diffraction depends on
the size of the gap compared to the
wavelength of the wave.

front:
What happens to the wavelength of
water waves in a ripple tank when the
frequency is reduced?
back:
When the frequency of water waves in a
ripple tank is reduced, the wavelength
increases.

front:
How do you decrease the wavelength of
water waves in a ripple tank?
back:
You decrease the wavelength of the
waves in a ripple tank by increasing the
frequency of the waves.

front:
True or False?
The image formed in a mirror is a real
image.
back:
False.
The image formed in a mirror is a
virtual image.

front:
True or False?
An image formed in a plane mirror will
be smaller than the object.
back:
False.
The image formed in a plane mirror will
be the same size as the object.

front: What is the normal?
back:
The normal is a line drawn
perpendicular (at 90°) to the boundary
of a material.

front:
True or False?
The image formed in a plane mirror will
be the same distance behind the mirror
as the object is in front of it.
back:
True.
The image formed in a plane mirror will
be the same distance behind the mirror
as the object is in front of it.

front:
Define the term angle of incidence for
light rays at the boundary of a material.
back:
The angle of incidence is the angle
between the incident ray and the
normal line at the boundary of a
material.

front:
True or False?
The image formed in a plane mirror will
be laterally inverted.
back:
True.
The image formed in a plane mirror will
be laterally inverted. The left hand side
of the object will appear on the right
hand side of the image and vice versa.

front: Define the term angle of reflection .
back:
The angle of reflection is the angle
between the reflected ray and the
normal at the boundary of a material.

front:
True or False?
The law of reflection applies to
reflection in plane mirrors.
back:
True.
The law of reflection is when the angle
of incidence is equal to the angle of
reflection and applies to a plane mirror.

front:
True or False?
An image formed in a plane mirror will
be virtual.
back:
True.
An image formed in a plane mirror will
be virtual.

front:
In an experiment to investigate
reflection by a plane mirror, what is the
independent variable? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
In an experiment to investigate
reflection by a plane mirror the
independent variable is the angle of
incidence.

front:
In an experiment to investigate
reflection by a plane mirror, what is the
dependent variable? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
The dependent variable in the reflection
investigation is the angle of reflection .

front:
In an experiment to investigate
reflection by a plane mirror, what
equipment is needed? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
In an experiment to investigate
reflection by a plane mirror the
equipment needed is:
a ray box
a protractor
a sheet of paper
a pencil
a ruler

front:
True or False?
Looking directly into a ray box the light
may damage the eyes. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
Looking directly into a ray box light may
damage the eyes.

front:
In an experiment to investigate
reflection by a plane mirror, what
results would you expect to find?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
In an experiment to investigate
reflection by a plane mirror, the results
you would expect to find are that the
angle of reflection is equal to the angle
of incidence at all angles tested.

front:
What action should be taken if a light
ray box causes burns? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
If the light ray box causes burns, the
burn should be held under cold running
water for at least five minutes.

front:
In an experiment to investigate
reflection by a plane mirror, which
factors should be controlled?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
In an experiment to investigate
reflection by a plane mirror, control
variables include:
distance of the ray box from the
mirror
width of the light beam
frequency/wavelength of the light

front:
True or False?
In an experiment to investigate
reflection by a plane mirror, an error
could occur in measuring the angles of
incidence and reflection if the normal
lines are not drawn perpendicular to
the surface of the mirror. This is an
example of a systematic error.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
Systematic errors are errors in the use
of apparatus or the experimental
method. Errors in measuring angles due
to drawing normal lines incorrectly are
systematic errors.

front:
True or False?
In an experiment to investigate
reflection by a plane mirror, a sharp
pencil should be used to mark the
centre of the beam to then draw the
ray. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
Using a sharp pencil and marking the
centre of the beam to then draw the ray
will reduce random errors in the results.

front:
What is the symbol for the angle of
incidence of a light ray on a boundary?
back:
The symbol for the angle of incidence of
a light ray on a boundary is i .

front:
What is the symbol for the angle of
refraction of a light ray on a boundary?
back:
The symbol for the angle of refraction of
a light ray on a boundary is r .

When light refracts by passing from a
less dense medium into a denser
medium, the ray bends away from the
normal.

False.
When light refracts by passing from a
less dense medium to a more dense
medium, it bends towards the normal.

front:

The frequency of light changes during
refraction.
back:
False.
The frequency of light does not change
during refraction.

When light passes along the normal,

True.

During refraction, the speed and

frequency.

glass block, how many boundary
surfaces does the ray pass through?
back:
In a ray diagram for refraction through

air-to-glass
glass-to-air

front:
True or False?
When light refracts through a glass
block, the incident ray at the boundary
of glass-to-air is the ray inside the glass.
back:
True.
When light refracts through a glass
block, the first boundary is air-to-glass,
and the second boundary is glass-to-air.
The refracted ray at the air-to-glass
boundary becomes the incident ray at
the glass-to-air boundary.

front:
Define refractive index. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
The refractive index is the ratio of the
speed of light in a vacuum and the
speed of light in a material.

front:
True or False?
The refractive index has no units.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
Since the refractive index is a ratio, it
has no units.

Snell's Law? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The trigonometric function used in
Snell's Law is sine.

When the angle of incidence i is

or i > r, the refracted ray bends toward
the normal.

The critical angle is the angle of

front:

occur?
back:
Total internal reflection (TIR) occurs
when the angle of incidence is greater
than the critical angle, and the ray is
travelling from a denser material into a
less dense material.

front:
How is total internal reflection used in
communications?
back:
Total internal reflection is used to
transmit information through optical
fibre cables for television and internet
communications.

for total internal reflection to occur?

front:
True or False?
A periscope is an example of an
application of total internal reflection.
back:
True.
In a periscope, two right-angled prisms
utilise total internal reflection to reflect
light.

front:
What is the refractive index of a
material?
back:
The refractive index is a measure of the
change in the speed of light as it travels
from a vacuum into a material. The
refractive index is a ratio, so it has no
units, and its value is always greater
than 1.

front:
True or False?
Total internal reflection can occur when
light travels from a less dense medium
into a denser medium.

False.
Total internal reflection only occurs
when light travels from a denser
material into a less dense material.

front: Define the term principal axis.
back:
The principal axis is a line which passes
through the centre of a lens.

front:
Define the term principal focus or
focal point.
back:
The principal focus or focal point, is the
point at which rays of light travelling
parallel to the principal axis intersect
the principal axis and converge at the
point where the diverging rays appear
to proceed.

front: Define the term focal length.
back:
Focal length is the distance between the
centre of the lens and the principal
focus.

front: What are the two types of lenses?
back:
The two types of lenses are:
converging lenses (convex)
diverging lenses (concave)

front:
True or False?
In a converging lens, parallel rays are
brought to a focus.
back:
True.
In a converging lens, parallel rays are
brought to a focus at a point called the
principal focus.

front:
True or False?
The more curved the converging lens,
the longer the focal length.
back:
False.
The more curved the converging lens is,
the shorter the focal length.

front:
True or False?
In a diverging lens, parallel rays are
made to diverge from a point.
back:
True.
In a diverging lens, parallel rays are
made to diverge (spread out) from a
point called the principal focus.

front:
What are the two types of images that
can be produced by lenses?
back:
The two types of images that can be
produced by lenses are:
real images
virtual images

front:
True or False?
Real images are always inverted.
back:
True.
Real images are always inverted.

front: Define the term real image.
back:
A real image is an image that is formed
when the light rays from an object
converge and meet each other and can
be projected onto a screen.

front:
True or False?
Real images cannot be projected onto a
screen.
back:
False.
Real images can be projected onto a
screen.

front: How is a real image produced?
back:
A real image is produced by the
convergence of light toward a focus.

front:
True or False?
Virtual images are always upright.
back:
True.
Virtual images are always upright.

front: Define the term virtual image.
back:
A virtual image is an image that is
formed when the light rays from an
object do not meet but appear to meet
behind the lens. Virtual images cannot
be projected onto a screen.

front:
True or False?
Virtual images can be projected onto a
screen.
back:
False.
Virtual images cannot be projected
onto a screen.

front: How are virtual images formed?
back:
Virtual images are formed by the
divergence of light away from a point.

front:
True or False?
A converging lens will form a real image
of an object if the object is placed at a
distance less than the focal length of
the lens.
back:
False.
A converging lens will form a real image
of an object if the object is placed at a
distance greater than the focal length
of the lens.

front:
True or False?
A converging lens will form a virtual
image of an object if the object is placed
at a distance less than the focal length
of the lens. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
A converging lens will form a virtual
image of an object if the object is placed
at a distance less than the focal length
of the lens.

front:
True or False?
Both converging and diverging lenses
are commonly used to correct defects
of sight. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
Both converging and diverging lenses
are commonly used to correct defects
of sight.

front:
True or False?
Short-sighted vision is caused by the
eye refracting light and bringing it to a
focal point in front of the retina.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
Short-sighted vision is caused by the
eye refracting light and bringing it to a
focal point in front of the retina.

front:
Which type of lens is used to correct
long-sighted vision? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Converging lenses are used to correct
long-sighted vision.

front:
Which type of lens is used to correct
short-sighted vision? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Diverging lenses are used to correct
short-sighted vision.

front:
Define the term short-sighted vision.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
People with short-sighted vision can
only see objects which are close to
them, they can not see objects which
are far away.

front:
Define the term long-sighted vision.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
People with long-sighted vision can only
see objects which are far away, they
cannot see objects which are close to
them.

front:
True or False?
Long-sighted vision is caused by the eye
refracting light and bringing it to a focal
point behind the retina. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
Long-sighted vision is caused by the eye
refracting light and bringing it to a focal
point behind the retina.

front:
True or False?
Convex lenses are used to correct the
vision of short-sighted people.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Convex or converging lenses are used
to correct the vision of long-sighted
people.

front:
True or False?
White light contains all the colours of
the visible spectrum.
back:
True.
White light contains all the colours of
the visible spectrum.

front:
Which spectrum is visible light a small
part of?
back:
Visible light is a small part of the
electromagnetic spectrum.

front:
What object can split white light into its
constituent colours when light passes
through it?
back:
A prism can be used to split white light
into its constituent colours when light is
passed through it.

front:
What is the name given to the process
of splitting white light into its
constituent colours?
back:
The process of splitting white light into
its constituent colours is called
dispersion.

front:
What type of wave behaviour causes
dispersion?
back:
Dispersion is caused by the refraction
of light through a prism. Violet light is
refracted the most and red light is
refracted the least.

front:
What are the seven colours that make
up white light?
back:
The seven colours that make up white
light are:
red
orange
yellow
green
blue
indigo
violet

front:
Which colour of the spectrum of visible
light has the longest wavelength?
back:
Red light has the longest wavelength of
all the colours in the visible spectrum.

front:
True or False?
Blue light has a longer wavelength than
yellow light.
back:
False.
Blue light has a shorter wavelength
than yellow light.

front:
True or False?
Orange light has a higher frequency
than violet light.
back:
False.
Orange light has a lower frequency
(and a longer wavelength) than violet
light.

front:
Define the term monochromatic light.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Monochromatic light is light with a
single frequency (or wavelength).

front: How are sound waves produced?
back:
Sound waves are produced by vibrating
(or oscillating) sources.

front:
What is the name of the region of a
sound wave that contains a lower
density of particles? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
The region of a sound wave that
contains a lower density of particles is
called a rarefaction.

front:
True or False?
Sound waves are transverse waves.
back:
False.
Sound waves are longitudinal waves.

front:
True or False?
Sound waves require a medium to
travel through.
back:
True.
Sound waves are longitudinal waves so
they do require a medium to travel
through.

front:
What is the name of the region of a
sound wave that contains a higher
density of particles? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
The region of a sound wave that
contains a higher density of particles is
called a compression.

front:
What is the difference between
compressions and rarefactions?
back:
Compressions are regions with a high
density of particles, while rarefactions
are regions with a low density of
particles.

front:
True or False?
Sound is a type of pressure wave.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
Sound is a type of pressure wave
consisting of compressions and
rarefactions, which cause changes in
pressure that vary with the wave.

front:
True or False?
Sound waves can travel through a
vacuum.
back:
False.
Sound waves require a medium to
travel through, so they cannot travel
through a vacuum where there are no
particles.

front:
What happens when sound waves hit a
solid? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
When sound waves hit a solid, the
variations in pressure cause the surface
of the solid to vibrate in sync with the
sound wave.

front: Define the speed of sound.
back:
The speed of sound is the speed which
sound travels through a particular
medium.

front:
What is the typical speed of sound in air
at room temperature?
back:
The speed of sound in air at room
temperature is about 340 m/s.

front:
True or False?
The speed of sound in air varies from
330 – 350 m/s.
back:
True.
The speed of sound in air varies from
330 – 350 m/s, with higher
temperatures leading to a greater
speed of sound.

front:
Through which state of matter does
sound travel the fastest? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Sound travels fastest in solids because
the particles in a solid are closer
together.

front:
Through which state of matter does
sound travel the slowest? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Sound travels the slowest in gases
because the particles are furthest apart.

front:
True or False?
Measuring the speed of sound using an
oscilloscope is the most accurate
method.
back:
True.
Measuring the speed of sound using an
oscilloscope is the most accurate
method because the timing is done
automatically.

front:
What is the relationship between the
frequency of a sound wave and its
pitch?
back:
Sounds with a high frequency (or short
wavelength) have a high pitch, and
sounds with a low frequency (or long
wavelength) have a low pitch.

What is the relationship between the
amplitude of a sound wave and its
volume?

Sounds with a large amplitude have a
high volume, and sounds with a small
amplitude have a low volume.

front:
True or False?
Decreasing the amplitude of a sound
wave will increase its volume.
back:
False.
Decreasing the amplitude of a sound
wave will decrease its volume.

front:
True or False?
Increasing the frequency of a sound
wave will increase its volume.
back:
False.
Increasing the frequency of a sound
wave will increase its pitch.

front:
How do you decrease the pitch of a
soundwave?
back:
Decreasing the frequency of a sound
wave will decrease the pitch of the
sound.

front:
What effect would increasing the
amplitude of a sound wave have on the
sound?
back:
Increasing the amplitude of a
soundwave would increase the volume
of the sound.

front: State the range of human hearing.
back:
The range of human hearing is 20 to 20
000 Hz.

front: Define the term ultrasound.
back:
Ultrasound is the name given to sound
waves with a frequency greater than
20,000 Hz.

front:
True or False?
Ultrasound is not audible to humans.
back:
True.
Ultrasound is not audible to humans
because it has a frequency greater than
20,000 Hz, which is beyond the range of
human hearing.

front:
What happens when ultrasound
reaches a boundary between two
media? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
When ultrasound reaches a boundary
between two media, some of the waves
are partially reflected, while the
remainder are transmitted through the
material.

front:
What is the typical range of human
hearing?
back:
Humans can hear sounds between
about 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz in
frequency, although this range
decreases with age.

front:
What do ultrasound transducers do?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Ultrasound transducers emit ultrasound
and receive ultrasound.

front:
What property of ultrasound allows it to
be used for medical and industrial
imaging? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The time taken for ultrasound
reflections to reach a detector can be
used to determine how far away a
boundary is, as ultrasound travels at
different speeds through different
media. This allows ultrasound waves to
be used for both medical and industrial
imaging.

front:
True or False?
Ultrasound is invasive and potentially
harmful. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Unlike many other medical imaging
techniques, ultrasound is non-invasive
and is believed to be harmless.

front:
True or False?
Ultrasound can be used to detect cracks
inside metal objects. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
In industry, ultrasound can be used to
check for cracks inside metal objects
and generate images beneath surfaces.

front:
True or False?
Ultrasound can be used to treat kidney
stones. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
Ultrasound can be used as a medical
treatment, such as removing kidney
stones.

front:
Can a human hear a sound with a
frequency of 18 kHz?
back:
Yes. Humans can detect sounds with
frequencies in the range of 20 Hz to 20
kHz.

front:
What is the name given to a group of
cells in an electric circuit?
back: A group of cells is called a battery.

front:
What is the difference between the
circuit symbols for a fixed resistor
a variable resistor?
back:
The symbol for a variable resistor has
and an arrow going through it, whereas the
symbol for a fixed resistor does not.

front:
What is the function of a relay in a
circuit?
back:
A relay uses a small current in one
circuit to switch on a much larger
current in another circuit.

front: What is a thermistor?
back:
A thermistor is a temperature-
dependent resistor.
This means its resistance changes
depending on its temperature.

front:
What is the effect of increased
temperature on a thermistor?
back:
When the temperature of a thermistor
is increased, its resistance decreases.

front: What does LDR stand for?
back:
LDR stands for light-dependent
resistor.

front:
What is the effect of increased light
intensity on an LDR?
back:
When light intensity on an LDR is
increased, its resistance decreases.
(Remember: Light Decreases Resistance
- LDR)

front:
True or False?
Current is different at different points in
a series circuit.
back:
False.
Current is the same everywhere in a
series circuit.

front:
True or False?
In a parallel circuit, the current from the
power source is larger than the current
in each branch.
back:
True.
In a parallel circuit, the current from the
power source is larger than the current
in each branch.

front:
True or False?
The amount of current flowing in a
series circuit depends on the potential
difference and resistance in the circuit.
back:
True.
The amount of current flowing in any
circuit depends on the potential
difference and resistance in the circuit.

front:
If the e.m.f. of the power source is
increased, but everything else in the
circuit remains constant, what effect
does this have on the current?
back:
If the e.m.f. (potential difference) of the
power source is increased, but
everything else in the circuit remains
constant, the current will increase.

front:
If the e.m.f. of the power source
remains constant, but more
components are added to a circuit,
what effect does this have on the
current?
back:
Adding components to a circuit
increases the total resistance of the
circuit, so the current would decrease
(for a constant e.m.f.).

front:
True or False?
One advantage of a parallel circuit is
that each bulb can be arranged in its
own branch with its own switch.
back:
True.
One advantage of a parallel circuit is
that each bulb can be arranged in its
own branch with its own switch.

front:
True or False?
One advantage of a series circuit is that
if one component stops working the
others will still work.
back:
False.
An advantage of parallel circuits is that
if components in one branch fail, the
components in other branches will still
work.
If one component fails in a series
circuit, then the circuit is broken and
the current cannot flow.

front:
True or False?
Current is conserved at a junction in a
parallel circuit. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
Current is conserved at a junction in a
parallel circuit because charge is always
conserved.

front:
True or False?
Current always splits equally at a
junction in a parallel circuit. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
False.
Current will only split equally at a
junction if the resistance in each
branch is equal.

front:
True or False?
When several cells are connected in
series, their combined e.m.f. is the
product of their individual e.m.f.s.
back:
False.
When several cells are connected in
series, their combined e.m.f. is the sum
of their individual e.m.f.s.

front:
What is the rule for determining the
potential difference in a series circuit?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The total potential difference across
the components in a series circuit is
equal to the sum of the individual
potential differences across each
component.

front:
What is the rule for determining the
potential difference in a parallel circuit?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The potential difference across an
arrangement of parallel resistances is
the same as the potential difference
across one branch in the arrangement
of the parallel resistances.

front:
What is the rule for calculating the
combined resistance of two or more
resistors in series?
back:
When two or more resistors are
connected in series, the combined
resistance is the sum of the individual
resistances.

front:
True or False?
The combined resistance of two
resistors in parallel is less than that of
either resistor by itself.
back:
True.
The combined resistance of two
resistors in parallel is less than that of
either resistor by itself.

front:
State the equation for calculating the
combined resistance of two resistors
connected in parallel. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
The equation for the combined
resistance of two resistors connected in
parallel is 1 = 1 + 1
R R 1 R 2
Where:
R = the total combined resistance,
measured in ohms (Ω)
R 1 = the resistance of the first
resistor, measured in ohms (Ω)
R 2 = the resistance of the second
resistor, measured in ohms (Ω)

front:
What is the function of a potential
divider? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
A potential divider splits the potential
difference of a power source between
two components.

front:
True or False?
When a potential divider is used in a
circuit, the resistor with the largest
resistance will have a greater potential
difference across it. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
When a potential divider is used in a
circuit, the resistor with the largest
resistance will have a greater
potential difference across it.

front:
What is a potentiometer? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
A potentiometer is a type of variable
resistor consisting of a coil of wire and
sliding contact.

front:
Give one application of a potential
divider. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Examples of applications of potential
dividers include:
volume controls
sensory circuits using LDRs
sensory circuits using thermistors

front:
What hazard does damaged insulation
on a wire pose?
back:
Exposed wires can cause electric
shocks if touched.

front:
What hazard does the overheating of
cables pose?
back:
Overheating of cables could lead to
melting of the insulation and exposing
the wires, or fires .

front:
Why is it dangerous to use electrical
circuits in damp conditions?
back:
Moisture can conduct electricity, so
using electric circuits in damp
conditions could lead to electric
shocks, or short circuits which may
damage the appliance or even start a
fire.

front:
Why is it dangerous to overload plugs,
extension leads and multiple sockets
when using the mains supply?
back:
If plug sockets are overloaded it can
lead to overheating which can cause
melting or even fires.

front:
True or False?
Mains circuits consist of a live wire, a
neutral wire and an earth wire.
back:
True.
Mains circuits do consist of a live wire, a
neutral wire and an earth wire.

front:
What circuit component must be
connected to the live wire in order for
the circuit to be turned off safely?
back:
A switch must be connected to the live
wire in order for the circuit to be turned
off safely.

front:
Why does the casing of an electrical
appliance have to be either non-
conducting or earthed?
back:
The casing of an electrical appliance
must be either non-conducting or
earthed to prevent the casing from
becoming electrified and causing an
electric shock to anyone who touches
it.

front: What is the purpose of a fuse?
back:
A fuse is a safety device designed to
break the circuit if the current exceeds
a certain amount.

front: What is the function of a trip switch?
back:
A trip switch is a switch on the
consumer unit that will break the
circuit if the current exceeds a certain
amount.

front:
True or False?
A fuse without an earth wire protects
the circuit and the cabling for a double-
insulated appliance.
back:
True.
A fuse without an earth wire protects
the circuit and the cabling for a double-
insulated appliance.

front:
How many types of electric charge are
there?
back:
There are two types of electric charge:
positive and negative.

front: Define electric charge.
back:
Electric charge is a property of matter
that causes it to experience
electromagnetic forces.

front:
True or False?
Opposite charges attract.
back:
True.
Opposite charges attract.

front:
What happens when two like charges
are brought close together?
back:
When two like charges are brought
close together, they repel each other.

front:
What does the saying "opposites-
attract" refer to in the context of
charges?
back:
The saying "opposites attract" refers to
the principle that opposite charges are
attracted to each other.

front:
What units are electric charges
measured in? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Electric charges are measured in units
called coulombs (C).

front: Define electrostatic repulsion.
back:
Electrostatic repulsion is the
phenomenon where like charges in an
electric field exert a force on one
another which pushes them apart.

front: What causes electrostatic repulsion?
back:
Electrostatic repulsion is caused by the
force between charges in an electric
field. When these charges are the same
the charges repel each other.

front:
What experiment can be used to
demonstrate the production of
electrostatic charges by friction?
back:
The experiment used to demonstrate
the production of electrostatic charges
by friction involves:
Suspending an insulating material
Rubbing it with a cloth to transfer
electrons from the surface
Observing its interaction with
another charged material

front: Define the term insulating solids.
back:
Insulating solids are materials that do
not conduct electricity easily and can
hold a static charge. Plastics are an
example of an insulating solid.

front:
What is the purpose of rubbing
insulating solids with a cloth in
electrostatic experiments?
back:
The purpose of rubbing insulating solids
with a cloth in electrostatic experiments
is to transfer electrons between the
cloth and the insulator leaving them
with opposing net charges.

front:
How can you determine if two charged
materials have the same charge?
back:
You can determine if two charged
materials have the same charge by
observing their interaction.
If they repel each other, they have
the same charge
If they attract, they have opposite
charges

front:
Define electric field. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
An electric field is the region
surrounding a charged object where
other charges will experience a force.
Field lines always point away from
positive charges and towards negative
charges.

front:
What does the direction of electric field
lines represent? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The direction of electric field lines
shows the direction a positive charge
would move if placed at that point.

front:
Describe how the strength of an electric
field changes with distance away from a
charged object. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The strength of an electric field
decreases with distance from a charged
object.

front:
Define a uniform electric field .
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
A uniform electric field is when the field
strength is constant and the field
lines are parallel and straight.

front:
Describe the properties of field lines
around a point charge. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
The properties of field lines around a
point charge are:
They extend radially outward
(away) from a positive charge and
radially inward (toward) a negative
charge.
They indicate the direction of the
force on a positively charged
particle at any given point in the
field.

front:
What is the nature of the electric field
between two parallel plates? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
The electric field between two parallel
plates is uniform, with field lines
directed from the positive to the
negative plate. The lines are parallel
and straight.

front:
What causes the symmetry of field lines
around a charged conducting sphere?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The symmetry of field lines around a
charged conducting sphere is due to the
even distribution of charges on the
sphere's surface, resulting in
symmetrical repulsion.

front:
True or False?
Electric fields always point towards
positive charges. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Electric fields always point away from
positive charges and towards negative
charges.

front:
True or False?
Conductors allow charge to move freely.
back:
True.
Conductors allow charge, usually
electrons, to move freely through them.

front: Define the term conductor.
back:
Conductors are materials that permit
the flow of charge, typically electrons,
with ease.

front:
True or False?
Metals are generally good insulators.
back:
False.
Metals are generally excellent
conductors due to their ability to
facilitate the flow of charge.

front:
True or False?
Copper is an example of a conductor.
back:
True.
Copper is an example of conductor.
Most electrical wiring is made of copper.

front:
What is the key difference between
conductors and insulators?
back:
The key difference between conductors
and insulators lies in their ability to
allow charge to move.
Conductors allow the movement of
charge, while insulators prevent it.

front:
State the properties of metal
conductors on an atomic scale.
back:
The properties of metal conductors on
an atomic scale are:
have a lattice structure (of metal
ions)
free (delocalised) electrons.

front: What are insulators?
back:
Insulators are materials that prevent
the flow of charge and instead
accumulate a build up of static charge.

front:
How can you distinguish between
conductors and insulators using a gold-
leaf electroscope?
back:
You can distinguish between
conductors and insulators using a gold-
leaf electroscope by:
Charging the plate of the gold-leaf
electroscope and then touching it
with the material being tested.
If the gold leaf falls, the material is a
good conductor.
If it remains in place, the material is
a poor conductor or insulator.

front:
What happens to the plate, rod and
gold leaf when the gold leaf
electroscope is charged?
back:
When the gold leaf electroscope is
charged the plate, rod and gold leaf all
have the same charge so they repel
each other and the gold leaf sticks out
to the side.

front: Define current.
back:
Current is the amount of charge
passing a fixed point per unit time.

front:
What is the equation for charge,
current, and time?
back:
The equation for charge, current, and
time is: Q = It
Where:
I = current, measured in amperes
(A)
Q = charge, measured in coulombs
(C)
t= time, measured in seconds (s)

front: What is the purpose of an ammeter?
back:
The purpose of an ammeter is to
measure the current in a circuit.

front:
True or False?
Ammeters should be connected in
parallel to measure current.
back:
False.
Ammeters should be connected in
series.

front:
What is conventional current?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Conventional current is the direction
that positive charge would flow around
a circuit, from the positive terminal to
the negative terminal.

front:
How is electron flow different to
conventional current? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Electrons flow around a circuit from the
negative terminal to the positive
terminal. This is the opposite direction
to conventional current.

front:
True or False?
Conventional current flows from
negative to positive. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
False. Conventional current is defined
as flowing from positive to negative,
even though electrons (negatively
charged) actually move in the opposite
direction.

front:
Which is most accurate, a digital or
analogue ammeter?
back:
A digital ammeter is more accurate than
an analogue ammeter because it has a
greater sensitivity, a larger range and
gives a definite numerical value.

front: What is direct current (d.c.)?
back:
Direct current flows in one direction
only.

front: What is alternating current (a.c.)?
back:
Alternating current continuously
changes direction.

front:
How can you distinguish between direct
and alternating current?
back:
You can distinguish between direct and
alternating current because:
direct current flows continuously
in one direction, typically from
negative to positive terminals
alternating current periodically
changes direction

back: The graphs for d.c. and a.c. are

front:
True or False?
Cells and batteries are sources of d.c.
back:
True.
Cells and batteries are sources of d.c.

front:
True or False?
An a.c. power source involves a positive
and negative terminal.
back:
False.
An a.c. power source involves two
identical terminals.

front:
True or False?
Electromotive force (e.m.f.) is the
potential difference of the power
source in a circuit.
back:
True.
Electromotive force (e.m.f.) refers to the
potential difference of the power source
in a circuit.

front: Define electromotive force (e.m.f.).
back:
Electromotive force (e.m.f.) is defined as
the electrical work done by the power
source in moving a unit charge around a
complete circuit. It is measured in volts
(V).

front:
What is the equation for electromotive
force (e.m.f.)? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The equation for electromotive force
(e.m.f.) is: E = W
Q
Where:
E = electromotive force, measured
in volts (V)
W = energy supplied from the
power source, measured in joules
(J)
Q = charge, measured in coulombs
(C)

front: Define potential difference .
back:
Potential difference is the the work
done by a unit charge passing through a
component.

front:
True or False?
Potential difference is measured in
amperes.
back:
False.
Potential difference is measured in
volts (V).

front: What is a voltmeter?
back:
A voltmeter is a device used to measure
the potential difference between two
points in an electrical circuit.

front:
True or False?
Voltmeters are connected in series with
the component being tested.
back:
False.
Voltmeters are connected in parallel
with the component being tested.

front:
What is the equation for potential
difference (p.d.), charge and work done?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The equation for potential difference
(p.d.), charge and work done is:
V = W
Q
Where:
V = potential difference, measured
in volts (V)
W = energy transferred to the
components, measured in joules (J)
Q = charge on each charge carrier,
measured in coulombs (C)

front:
True or False?
Resistance is a measure of how difficult
it is for current to pass through a
conductor or component.
back:
True.
Resistance is a measure of how difficult
it is for current to pass through a
conductor or component.

front: Define Ohm's law.
back:
Ohm's Law states that the current
flowing through a conductor is directly
proportional to the potential difference
across the conductor.

front: What is the equation for Ohm's law?
back:
The equation for Ohm's law is: V = IR
Where:
R = resistance, measured in ohms
(Ω)
V = potential difference, measured
in volts (V)
I = current, measured in amperes
(A)

front:
True or False?
The unit of resistance is volts.
back:
False.
The unit of resistance is the ohm,
represented by the Greek symbol
omega (Ω).

front:
What is an I-V graph? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
An I-V graph, or current-voltage graph,
is a graphical representation of the
relationship between the current
flowing through a component and the
potential difference across it. It shows
how the current changes with potential
difference.

front:
What is the shape of the I-V graph for a
fixed resistor? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The shape of the I-V graph for a fixed
resistor is a straight line passing
through the origin, indicating that the
current is directly proportional to the
potential difference.

front:
True or False?
A diode is a non-ohmic conductor.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
A diode is a non-ohmic conductor. This
means current and potential difference
are not directly proportional.

front:
What is the unique characteristic of a
diode's I-V graph? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The unique characteristic of an I-V
graph for a diode is a sharp increase in
current when it is in forward bias, and a
flat line indicating zero current when it
is in reverse bias.

front: Define the resistance of a wire.
back:
The resistance of a wire is the
opposition encountered by electrons as
they pass through a wire due to
collisions with metal ions. It is a
measure of how difficult it is for current
to flow through the wire.

front:
How does the length of a wire affect its
resistance? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The resistance of a wire is directly
proportional to its length. This means
that as the length of the wire increases,
its resistance also increases by the
same factor.

front:
How does the cross-sectional area of a
wire affect its resistance? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
The resistance of a wire is inversely
proportional to its cross-sectional area.
As the wire's cross-sectional area
(thickness) increases, its resistance
decreases, and vice versa.

front:
True or False?
If a wire is thicker, its resistance is
greater. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
If a wire is thicker (greater diameter), its
resistance is less.

front:
True or False?
If a wire is longer, its resistance is
higher. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
If a wire is longer, its resistance is higher
because each electron will collide with
more ions along the wire's length,
resulting in a greater opposition to the
flow of electrons.

front:
If the length of a wire is increased by a
factor of 3, what is the effect on its
resistance? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The resistance of a wire is directly
proportional to its length, so if the
length is increased by a factor of 3, the
resistance will increase by a factor of 3.

front:
If the cross-sectional area of a wire is
halved what is the effect on its
resistance? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The resistance of a wire is inversely
proportional to its cross-sectional area,
therefore if its cross-sectional area is
halved, its resistance will double.

front: Define electrical energy.
back:
Electrical energy is the energy
transferred by an electric current.
This is typically from a power source to
the components connected in an
electrical circuit, where it is transformed
into other stores of energy, such as
thermal or kinetic energy.

front:
True or False?
Energy transferred in a circuit is related
to potential difference, current, and
time. as described by the equation
back:
True.
Potential difference, current, and time
are related in electrical energy transfer,
E = V × I × t .

front: What is the electrical energy equation?
back:
The electrical energy equation is:
E = V × I × t
Where:
E = electrical energy transferred,
measured in joules (J)
V = voltage supplied, measured in
volts (V)
I = current, measured in amperes
(A)
t = time, measured in seconds (s)

front: How is energy transferred in a circuit?
back:
In a circuit, energy is transferred from
the power source to the components
connected in the circuit.
As charge passes through the power
supply, it gains energy in its kinetic
store, which is then transferred to the
energy stores of the components as it
passes through them.

front:
What two factors affect the amount of
energy transferred in an appliance?
back:
The amount of energy transferred in an
appliance depends on:
How long the appliance is switched
on for
The power rating of the appliance

front: What does the unit kW mean?
back:
The unit kW stands for kilowatt, equal
to 1000 watts.

front:
True or False?
Energy in a circuit is transferred from
the power source to the components
and the surroundings.
back:
True.
Energy in a circuit is transferred from
the power source to the components
and the surroundings.

front:
What are the main energy transfers in a
toaster while it toasts a slice of bread?
back:
In a toaster:
Electrical energy is transferred from the
mains supply to the thermal store of
the heating element and then to the
thermal store of the bread.

front:
What are the main energy transfers in a
washing machine while on a washing
cycle?
back:
Electrical energy is transferred from the
mains supply to the kinetic store of the
motor, to the kinetic store of the drum
as it spins.

front: Define electrical power.
back:
Electrical power is defined as the rate at
which electrical energy is transferred or
converted per unit of time, typically
measured in watts (W).

front:
True or False?
Power is the rate of doing work.
back:
True.
Power is defined as the rate of doing
work, or, the rate of energy transfer.
It is typically measured in watts (W).

front: What is the electrical power equation?
back:
The electrical power equation is:
P = I × V
Where:
P = power, measured in watts (W)
V = voltage, measured in volts (V)
I = current, measured in amperes
(A)

front:
How is electrical power related to work
done in a circuit?
back:
Power is defined as the rate of doing
work.
Therefore, electrical power describes
the rate at which electrical energy is
transferred or converted.

front:
State the equation for calculating
electrical power in terms of resistance.
back:
The equation for electrical power in
terms of resistance is: P = I2 × R
Where:
P = power, measured in watts (W)
I = current, measured in amperes
(A)
R = resistance, measured in ohms
(Ω)

front:
True or False?
The unit of power is joules (J).
back:
False.
The unit of power is watts (W), where 1
watt is equivalent to 1 joule per second.

front:
What does the unit kilowatt hour
(kWh) mean?
back:
The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of
energy. It is equivalent to one kilowatt
of power expended for one hour.
It is commonly used to measure and
compare energy usage in homes and
businesses.

front:
True or False?
Energy usage in homes is measured in
joules (J).
back:
False.
Energy usage in homes and businesses
is commonly measured in kilowatt-
hours (kWh), where 1 kWh is the energy
consumed using 1 kilowatt of power for
1 hour.

front:
What is the equation that defines the
kilowatt hour (kWh)?
back:
The equation that defines the kilowatt
hour (kWh) is: E = P × t
Where:
E = energy, measured in kilowatt-
hours (kWh)
P = power, measured in kilowatts
(kW)
t = time, measured in hours (h)

front: What is electromagnetic induction?
back:
Electromagnetic induction is the effect
of inducing e.m.f. in a conductor due
to the relative motion between a
conductor and a magnetic field .

front: How can an e.m.f. be induced in a wire?
back:
An e.m.f. be induced in a wire by
moving it through a magnetic field.

front:
True or False?
An e.m.f. can only be induced by
moving a conductor in a magnetic field.
back:
False.
An e.m.f. can also be induced by placing
a stationary conductor in a changing
magnetic field.

front:
How can the direction of an induced
e.m.f. be reversed?
back:
The direction of an induced e.m.f. can
be reversed by:
Reversing the direction of motion
(of the magnet or conductor)
Swapping the poles of the magnet

front:
Define Lenz's Law. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Lenz's Law states that the direction of
an induced e.m.f. always opposes the
change producing it.

front:
How can Lenz's Law be demonstrated?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Lenz's Law can be demonstrated using
a bar magnet and a coil of wire.
When the magnet moves into or out of
a coil of wire, the induced e.m.f. creates
a magnetic field that opposes the
motion of the magnet.

front:
True or False?
When the north pole of a bar magnet is
pushed towards a coil, the end of the
coil begins to act as a south pole.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
When the north pole of a bar magnet is
pushed towards a coil, the end of the
coil begins to act as a north pole.
As a result, the two like poles repel in
order to oppose the motion of the
magnet.

front:
What is the Right-Hand Dynamo rule?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The Right-Hand Dynamo rule is used to
determine the direction of an induced
e.m.f in a wire moving through a
magnetic field.

front:
When using the Right-Hand Dynamo
rule, what does the first finger
represent? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
When using the Right-Hand Dynamo
rule, the first finger represents the
direction of the magnetic field from
the north pole to the south pole.

front:
True or False?
When using the Right-Hand Dynamo
rule, the second finger always indicates
the flow of current from the positive
terminal to the negative terminal of the
battery. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
When using the Right-Hand Dynamo
rule, the second finger always indicates
the direction of positive charge
carriers or the flow of current from the
positive terminal to the negative
terminal of the battery.

demonstrated using a wire and a U-

back:

Moving the wire up or down

Moving the magnet up or down
