front:
What apparatus can be used to
determine if an e.m.f. has been induced
in a conductor?
back:
A sensitive voltmeter or ammeter can
be used to determine if an e.m.f. has
been induced in a conductor.

front:
True or False?
An e.m.f. is induced when a wire moves
up and down between the poles of a
stationary magnet.
back:
True.
For electromagnetic induction to occur,
there must be relative motion between
the conductor and the magnetic field.
Therefore, an e.m.f. is induced when a
wire moves up and down between the
poles of a stationary magnet.

front:
True or False?
An e.m.f. is induced when a coil and a
bar magnet move in the same direction
at the same speed.
back:
False.
For electromagnetic induction to occur,
there must be relative motion between
the conductor and the magnetic field.
Therefore, an e.m.f. is not induced
when a coil and a bar magnet move in
the same direction at the same speed.

front:
What three factors affect the
magnitude of an induced e.m.f.?
back:
Three factors that affect the magnitude
of an induced e.m.f. are:
The speed of motion of the
magnet or coil
The number of turns on the coil
The strength of the magnet

front:
True or False?
The size of the induced e.m.f. across a
conductor is directly proportional to the
rate at which it cuts magnetic field lines.
back:
True.
The size of the induced e.m.f. across a
conductor is directly proportional to the
rate at which it cuts magnetic field lines.

front:
How can the size of the induced e.m.f.
be increased using a wire and a U-
shaped magnet?
back:
The induced e.m.f. can be increased
using a wire and a U-shaped magnet by:
increasing the length of the wire
between the poles, or using a
magnet with wider poles
moving the wire between the
magnet poles faster
increasing the strength of the
magnet

front:
How can the size of the induced e.m.f.
be increased in the experiment using a
coil and a bar magnet?
back:
The induced e.m.f. can be increased
using a coil and a bar magnet by:
adding more turns to the coil
moving the magnet into the coil
faster
increasing the strength of the
magnet

front:
True or False?
The number of paper clips attracted by
a strong electromagnet can be
increased by reducing the number of
coils of wire.
back:
False.
The number of paper clips attracted by
a strong electromagnet can be
increased by increasing the number of
coils of wire.

front:
What is an A.C. generator? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
An A.C. generator is a device which
converts energy from a mechanical
store to an electrical store.

front:
What is the output of an A.C.
generator? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The output of an A.C. generator is
alternating current.

front:
What components make up a simple
A.C. generator? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
A simple A.C. generator consists of:
1. A rectangular coil of wire rotating in
a magnetic field
2. Slip rings and brushes

front:
What is the purpose of the slip rings?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The purpose of slip rings is to provide a
connection between the rotating coil
and the external circuit.

front:
How often does the direction of the
current reverse as an A.C. generator
rotates? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The direction of the current reverses
every half rotation of the coil in the
A.C. generator.

front:
True or False?
A maximum value of current is induced
when the coil is parallel to the magnetic
field. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
A maximum value of current is induced
when the coil is perpendicular to the
magnetic field.

front:
True or False?
There is a point in the rotation of the
coil where no current is induced.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
No current is induced when the coil is
parallel to the field.

front:
What is the shape of the graph of
output current against time for an A.C.
generator? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
For an A.C. generator, the shape of the
graph of output current against time is
a sine or cosine curve.

front:
What is the frequency of an A.C. output?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The frequency of an A.C. output is the
number of complete cycles it makes
each second e.g. 1 cycle per second = 1
Hz.

front:
How can the size of the induced current
be increased in an A.C. generator?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
In an A.C. generator, the size of the
induced current can be increased by:
adding more turns to the coil
rotating the coil faster
increasing the strength of the
magnet

front:
What is the pattern of the magnetic
field due to the current in a straight
wire?
back:
The magnetic field due to a current in a
straight wire forms concentric circles
that get further apart with increasing
distance from the wire.

front:
What rule is used to determine the
direction of the magnetic field around a
current carrying wire?
back:
The right-hand thumb rule can be
used to determine the direction of the
magnetic field around a current-
carrying wire.

front:
What pattern is formed by the magnetic
field inside a current-carrying solenoid?
back:
Inside a solenoid, the magnetic field is
uniform, so the field lines are equally
spaced straight lines pointing in the
same direction.

front:
True or False?
When viewed from the end of a
solenoid, the pole is a north pole if the
current travels clockwise around the
coil.
back:
False.
When viewed from the end of a
solenoid, the pole is a south pole if the
current travels clockwise around the
coil.

front:
How can the strength of the magnetic
field around a solenoid be increased?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The strength of the magnetic field
around a solenoid can be increased by:
increasing the current
increasing the number of turns on
the coil
adding a soft iron core to the centre
of the coil

front:
Changing the direction of the current
through a solenoid would have what
effect on the magnetic field around it?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Changing the direction of the current
through a solenoid would change the
direction of the magnetic field around
it.

front:
Describe when a force on a current-
carrying conductor occurs.
back:
A current-carrying conductor in the
presence of a magnetic field
experiences a force, resulting in its
movement or deflection.

front:
True or False?
A current-carrying conductor will only
experience a force if the current is
parallel to the magnetic field lines.
back:
False.
A current-carrying conductor will only
experience a force if the current
through it is perpendicular to the
direction of the magnetic field lines.

front:
What is Fleming's left-hand rule used
for? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Fleming's left-hand rule is used to
determine the direction of the force
acting on a current-carrying conductor
in a magnetic field, as well as the
direction of the current and magnetic
field.

front:
State the quantity represented by each
finger in Fleming's left-hand rule.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The quantity represented by each finger
in Fleming's left-hand rule is:
First finger is the direction of the
magnetic field
Second finger is the direction of
the current in the wire
Thumb is the direction of the force
which shows the direction of the
movement of the wire

front:
True or False?
The direction of the force on a current-
carrying wire depends on the direction
of the current and the magnetic field.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
The direction of the force on a current-
carrying wire depends on the direction
of the current and the direction of the
magnetic field, both of which should be
perpendicular to each other.

front:
Where does the maximum force
experienced by a charged particle
entering a magnetic field occur?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The maximum force experienced by a
charged particle entering a magnetic
field occurs when the particle is
traveling perpendicular to the field
lines.

front:
Describe the behaviour of moving
charged particles in a magnetic field.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Charged particles in a magnetic field
experience a force which causes them
to deflect .

front:
What can be used to determine the
direction of the force experienced by
an electron in a magnetic field?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The direction of the force experienced
by an electron in a magnetic field can be
determined using Fleming's left-hand
rule, where the second finger
(representing current) points opposite
to the direction of electron flow.

front:
What can the motor effect be used to
create?
back:
The motor effect can be used to create
a simple d.c. electric motor.

front: Describe a simple d.c. electric motor.
back:
A simple d.c. electric motor consists of a
coil of wire (which is free to rotate)
positioned in a uniform magnetic field.

front:
What causes the coil in a d.c. motor to
rotate?
back:
The coil in a d.c. motor rotates due to
experiencing a force (and therefore a
turning effect) when an electric current
flows through it in a magnetic field.

front:
True or False?
The split-ring commutator swaps the
contacts of the coil.
back:
True.
Every half turn, the pair of split rings
swap contact with the brushes.

front:
What does the split-ring commutator do
to the current?
back:
The split-ring commutator reverses the
direction of the current in the coil of a
d.c. motor every half-turn, ensuring
continuous rotation as long as the
current flows.

front:
What factors affect the speed of
rotation of a d.c. motor?
back:
The factors that affect the speed of
rotation of a d.c. motor are:
increasing the current through the
rotating coil
using a stronger magnet on either
side of the rotating coil

front:
What changes the direction of rotation
of the coil in a d.c. motor?
back:
The direction of rotation of the coil in a
d.c. motor can be changed by:
reversing the direction of the
current
reversing the poles of the magnet

front:
What increases the force supplied by a
d.c. motor?
back:
The force supplied by a d.c. motor is
increased by:
increasing the current in the coil
increasing the strength of the
magnetic field
adding more turns to the coil

front:
How can you determine the direction of
rotation of the coil in a d.c. motor?
back:
You determine the direction of rotation
of the coil in a d.c. motor by:
drawing arrows for the direction of
the magnetic field and current
using Fleming's left-hand rule to
find the force direction
determining the direction of
rotation of the coil based on the
forces

The function of a transformer is to

A simple transformer consists of:

front: Define the term magnet.
back:
Magnets are objects with north and
south poles. They attract magnetic
materials and can attract or repel other
magnets.

front: Name the two poles of a magnet.
back:
The two poles of a magnet are the
north and south poles.

front:
True or False?
Opposite poles attract.
back:
True.
Opposite poles attract.

front:
Define the meaning of the phrase
poles.
back:
like Like poles have the same polarity (e.g.
north and north) and they repel each
other.

front:
Define the meaning of the phrase
unlike poles.
back:
Unlike poles have opposite polarities
(e.g. north and south) and attract each
other.

front:
What does it mean for a material to be
magnetic?
back:
A magnetic material experiences an
attractive force when placed in a
magnetic field and can be magnetised
to form a magnet.

front:
State the meaning of the term non-
magnetic material.
back:
Non-magnetic materials do not
experience a force when placed in a
magnetic field.

front:
True or False?
Only a magnet can repel another
magnet.
back:
True.
Only a magnet can repel another
magnet.

front: What is the test for a magnet?
back:
To test whether a material is a magnet,
it should be brought close to a known
magnet. If it can be repelled by the
known magnet, then the material itself
is a magnet.

front:
True or False?
The south pole of one magnet repels
the north pole of another magnet.
back:
False.
Opposite poles attract.

front: Define the term permanent magnet.
back:
Permanent magnets produce their own
magnetic field and do not lose their
magnetism.

front: What is induced magnetism?
back:
Induced magnetism is when a magnetic
material is placed in a magnetic field
and the material can temporarily be
turned into a magnet.

front: Define the term magnetic material.
back:
Magnetic materials are materials that
are attracted to a magnet.

front:
True or False?
Induced magnets retain their
magnetism after being removed from
the magnetic field.
back:
False.
Induced magnets lose most/all of their
magnetism quickly after being removed
from the magnetic field.

front:
What happens to the ends of a
magnetic material when it becomes an
induced magnet?
back:
When magnetism is induced in a
material, one end of the material will
become a north pole, and the other end
will become a south pole.

front:
True or False?
Aluminium is a magnetic material.
back:
False.
Aluminium is not a magnetic material.

front:
What is an example of a magnetic
material?
back:
Iron, cobalt, nickel, and steel (an alloy
containing iron) are examples of
magnetic materials.

front:
How can you determine which pole is
induced at a particular end of a
magnetic material?
back:
To determine which pole is induced at
one end of a magnetic material, hold a
south pole near that end. If the end is
repelled, it is a south pole. If it attracts,
it is a north pole.

front:
What is an example of a non-magnetic
material?
back:
Any material other than iron, cobalt,
nickel, and steel (or alloys containing
these metals) is a non-magnetic
material. For example, aluminum,
copper, wood, plastic, etc.

front:
True or False?
The south pole of an induced magnet
will repel an iron paperclip.
back:
False.
The iron paperclip, a magnetic material,
can only be attracted by a magnet, not
repelled.

front: Define the term magnetic field .
back:
A magnetic field is the region around a
magnet where a force acts on another
magnet or on a magnetic material.

front:
Define the term uniform magnetic
field.
back:
A uniform magnetic field is a magnetic
field that has the same strength and
direction at all points.

front:
How is a uniform magnetic field
represented in diagrams?
back:
In a uniform magnetic field, the
magnetic field lines are equally spaced,
and all arrows point in the same
direction.

front: What are magnetic field lines?
back:
Magnetic field lines are lines drawn to
represent the strength and direction of
a magnetic field.

front:
What are the two rules for drawing
magnetic field lines?
back:
Two rules for drawing magnetic field
lines are:
1. Magnetic field lines must always go
from north to south (indicated by
an arrow midway along the line)
2. Field lines must never touch or
cross other field lines

front:
True or False?
The magnetic field is strongest at the
poles of a bar magnet.
back:
True.
The magnetic field is strongest at the
poles of a bar magnet, where the
magnetic field lines are closest together.

front:
What do closely spaced magnetic field
lines indicate? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Closely spaced magnetic field lines
indicate a strong magnetic field.

front:
What do widely spaced magnetic field
lines indicate? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Widely spaced magnetic field lines
indicate a weak magnetic field.

front:
What causes magnetic forces?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Magnetic forces are caused by
interactions between magnetic fields.

front:
The magnetic field of a bar magnet gets
weaker further from the magnet. How is
this represented in a diagram?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
To represent the fact that a bar
magnet's field weakens with distance
from the magnet, the field lines get
further apart further from the bar
magnet.

front:
What are the two principal ways of
plotting the magnetic field around a bar
magnet?
back:
The two principal ways of plotting the
magnetic field around a bar magnet are
using iron filings and using plotting
compasses.

front:
What is the method for plotting
magnetic field lines using iron filings?
back:
To plot magnetic field lines using iron
filings:
1. Place a piece of paper on top of the
magnet
2. Gently sprinkle iron filings on top of
the paper
3. Carefully tap the paper to allow the
iron filings to settle on the field
lines

front:
What is the method for plotting
magnetic field lines using a plotting
compass?
back:
To plot magnetic field lines using a
plotting compass:
1. Place the magnet on top of a piece
of paper and draw a dot at one end
2. Place a plotting compass next to
the dot so that one end of the
needle points towards the dot
3. Draw a new dot at the other side of
the compass needle
4. Move the compass to point towards
the new dot
5. Repeat the process to create a
chain of dots representing the
magnetic field line

front:
True or False?
The direction of the magnetic field line
plotted using a compass is the same as
the direction of the plotting compass.
back:
True.
The direction of the magnetic field line
plotted using a compass is the same as
the direction of the plotting compass.

front:
What do you need to do after creating a
chain of dots using a plotting compass?
back:
After creating a chain of dots using a
plotting compass, you need to remove
the compass and link the dots using a
smooth curve to represent the magnetic
field line.

front:
How can you plot multiple magnetic
field lines around a bar magnet?
back:
To plot multiple magnetic field lines
around a bar magnet, you need to
repeat the process of using the plotting
compass several times, starting from
different points on the magnet.

front:
True or False?
The compass needle points in the
opposite direction to the arrows on the
field lines.
back:
False.
The needle points in the same direction
as the arrows on the field lines.

front:
True or False?
In the iron filing experiment, more
filings will gather near the magnet's
poles than at the edge of the paper.
back:
True.
The magnetic field is stronger at the
magnet's poles, so more iron filings will
gather here.

front: Define background radiation.
back:
Background radiation is the radiation
that exists around us all the time.

front:
True or False?
Radiation is solely a human-made
phenomenon.
back:
False.
Radiation is a natural phenomenon that
has always existed on Earth and in
outer space.

front:
What are the natural sources of
background radiation?
back:
Natural sources of background
radiation include:
radon gas
cosmic rays from space
radioactive elements in rocks and
soil

front:
True or False?
Ionising nuclear radiation can be
measured using a detector connected
to an emitter.
back:

Ionising nuclear radiation can be
measured using a detector connected
to a counter.

front: What are the units of count rate?
back:
Count rate is measured in counts per
second or counts per minute.

front:
True or False?
A corrected count rate can be
calculated by adding the count rate
found with no radioactive source
present to the count rate with the
radioactive source present. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
False.
A corrected count rate can be calculated
by subtracting the count rate found
with no radioactive source present from
the count rate with the radioactive
source present. (Extended Tier Only)

front:
Does the count rate increase or
decrease as the detector moves further
from the radiation source?
back:
The count rate decreases as the
detector moves further from the
radiation source.

front:
What is the procedure for determining
background radiation count. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
To determine background radiation
count, move the radiation source back
until the count rate remains constant,
indicating only background radiation,
then record the count rate.

front:
True or False?
The emission of radiation from a
nucleus is spontaneous and occurs
randomly.
back:
True.
The emission of radiation from a
nucleus is spontaneous and occurs
randomly.

front:
What are the three types of radiation
that a nucleus can emit?
back:
The three types of radiation that a
nucleus can emit are:
alpha (α )
beta (β )
gamma (γ )

front:
True or False?
Nuclear decay is predictable and
organised.
back:
False.
Nuclear decay is spontaneous and
random.

front:
True or False?
It is possible to predict when a nucleus
will decay but not which nucleus will
decay.
back:
False.
It is not possible to predict when a
nucleus will decay or which nucleus will
decay. But it is possible to estimate
how many nuclei will decay, or the
probability that a nucleus will decay in
a given time frame.

front:
What is the composition of an alpha
particle?
back:
An alpha particle is composed of two
protons and two neutrons. It is
essentially a helium nucleus.

front:
What is the composition of a beta
particle?
back:
A beta particle is composed of a fast-
moving electron.

front:
True or False?
Alpha particles have a charge of -1.
back:
False.
Alpha particles have a charge of +2 due
to having two positively charged
protons. It is beta particles that have a
charge of -1 due to the negatively
charged electron.

front:
Which type of nuclear radiation is the
most ionising?
back:
Alpha particles are the most ionising
form of nuclear radiation. Beta particles
are next, and gamma radiation is the
least ionising.

front:
What are the types of nuclear radiation
in order of increasing penetrating
power?
back:
The types of nuclear radiation in order
of increasing penetrating power are:
alpha (least penetrating, can be
stopped by paper)
beta (can stopped by a few mm of
aluminium)
gamma (most penetrating, can be
reduced by a few mm of lead)

front:
Why are alpha particles the most
ionising of all the types of nuclear
radiation? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Alpha particles have the greatest
charge of all the nuclear decay
radiation at +2. Therefore, they attract
electrons from other atoms very
strongly. Alpha particles also have the
greatest mass, and therefore a high
kinetic energy. These factors
combined make alpha particles highly
ionising.

front:
Why is gamma radiation the least
ionising of all the types of nuclear
radiation? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Gamma radiation has no charge so it is
less ionising than alpha and beta
particles. However, gamma radiation is
still capable of ionising atoms as it is the
highest energy electromagnetic wave.
(Remember that UV, X-rays and gamma
rays are ionising.)

front:
Why are beta particles ionising?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Beta particles have a negligible mass,
but they travel at very high speeds. This
means that they have a high kinetic
energy. Beta (minus) particles also have
a charge of -1 so they repel electrons,
knocking them out of atoms. These
factors combined make them ionising.

front:
Which types of nuclear radiation can be
deflected in an electric field? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Nuclear radiation can be deflected in an
electric field if it has charge. Therefore,
alpha and beta particles can be
deflected in an electric field.

front:
True or False?
Alpha particles in an electric field will be
deflected toward the positively charged
plate. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Alpha particles are positively charged
and opposite charges attract, therefore
alpha particles will deflect toward the
negatively charged plate in an electric
field.

front:
True or False?
Gamma radiation cannot be deflected
by electric or magnetic fields.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
Gamma radiation has no charge
therefore it cannot be deflected by
electric or magnetic fields.

front:
Are alpha or beta particles deflected the
most when travelling through an
electric field? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Beta particles are deflected the most
when travelling through an electric field.
Alpha particles have a greater mass so
they get deflected the least.

front:
True or False?
The most stable nuclei have
approximately equal numbers of
protons and neutrons. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
The most stable nuclei have
approximately equal numbers of
protons and neutrons.

front:
True or False?
A nucleus becomes stable by reducing
its overall nuclear energy. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
True.
A nucleus becomes stable by reducing
its overall nuclear energy. It does this by
emitting high-energy alpha and beta
particles and gamma radiation.

front:
What two factors can cause an isotope
to be radioactive? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The two factors that can cause an
isotope to be radioactive are:
an excess of neutrons in the
nucleus
the nucleus being too heavy

front:
Which types of nuclear decay cause the
isotope to decay into a new element?
back:
An isotope will decay into a new
element if the number of protons
changes. Therefore, alpha and beta
decay will produce a new element.

front:
By what value does the mass number
decrease as a result of alpha decay?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Alpha decay results in the mass
number decreasing by 4, because 4
nucleons are emitted.

front:
True or False?
In beta decay, a neutron changes into a
proton and an electron. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
A neutron changes into a proton and
an electron during beta decay. The
high-energy electron is emitted from
the nucleus.

front:
By what value does the atomic number
decrease as a result of alpha decay?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Alpha decay results in the atomic
number decreasing by 2, because 2
protons are emitted.

front:
How are the mass and atomic numbers
affected by gamma decay? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Gamma decay has no effect on the
mass number or the atomic number.
Gamma radiation reduces the energy
of the nucleus but has no effect on the
number of particles.

front:
By what value does the atomic number
change as a result of beta decay?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The atomic number increases by 1 as
a result of beta decay. A neutron
changes into a proton and an electron.
The extra proton causes the atomic
number to increase by 1, so a new
element is formed.

front:
By what value does the charge on a
nucleus decrease when it emits an
alpha particle? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The charge on a nucleus will decrease
by 2 after it emits an alpha particle
because 2 protons are emitted.

front:
By what value does the mass number
decrease as a result of beta decay?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The mass number remains unchanged
by beta decay. A neutron changes into
a proton which has the same mass. A
beta particle is emitted but this change
in mass is negligible.

front: Define the term half-life.
back:
Half-life is the time taken for half the
nuclei of a particular isotope in any
sample to decay.

front:
True or False?
The half-life for a particular isotope is
always the same.
back:
True.
Half-life is constant for any particular
isotope.

front:
How is the activity of a radioactive
sample affected after one half-life?
back:
The activity of a radioactive sample will
have halved after one half-life

front:
True or False?
Half-life is different for different
isotopes.
back:
True.
Half-life is different for different
isotopes.

front:
What is the symbol for activity on a half-
life graph?
back:
The symbol for activity on a half-life
graph is A .

front:
What is the value of the activity of a
radioactive sample after two half-lives?
back:
The value of the activity of a radioactive
sample after two half-lives is 1 of its
4
original value.

front:
What is the symbol for original activity
on a half-life graph?
back:
The symbol for original activity on a
half-life graph is A 0.

front:
How do you determine the half-life of
an isotope on a graph of activity over
time?
back:
To determine the half-life of an isotope
on a graph of activity over time:
identify the point at which the
activity has halved and draw a line
to the curve
track that point down to the time
axis

front:
What proportion of original nuclei in a
radioactive sample will remain after
three half-lives?
back:
After three half-lives, the proportion of
original nuclei remaining in the sample
will be 1 .

front:
When determining the activity of a
radioactive sample, how do you adjust
for background radiation? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
When determining the activity of a
radioactive sample, the count rate of
the background radiation must be
subtracted from the activity of the
sample.

front:
Which type of nuclear radiation is used
in smoke detectors? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Alpha radiation is used in smoke
detectors.

front:
Which type of nuclear radiation is used
for measuring and controlling the
thickness of materials? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Beta radiation is used in measuring and
controlling the thickness of materials.

front:
Which type of nuclear radiation is used
for irradiating food to kill bacteria?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Gamma radiation is used for irradiating
food to kill bacteria.

front:
Which type of nuclear radiation is used
for sterilising equipment? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Gamma radiation is used for sterilising
equipment.

front:
How does a smoke alarm work?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
A smoke alarm works as follows:
alpha particles ionise the air inside
the detector creating a current
the alpha emitter is blocked by the
presence of smoke particles
the alarm is triggered when the
sensor no longer detects alpha
particles

front:
Why are alpha particles not used to
detect the thickness of materials?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Alpha particles are stopped by paper,
so they would not penetrate the
material to reach the detector.

front:
Why is gamma radiation used in the
sterilisation of food and equipment?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Gamma radiation can penetrate
packaging and objects so all surfaces of
the food or equipment can be
irradiated. Gamma radiation is
ionising enough to kill any
microorganism, therefore it is used for
sterilisation.

front:
Why are beta particles used to detect
the thickness of materials? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Beta particles can penetrate materials
such as paper and aluminium foil, so
the number of beta particles detected
by a sensor can be used to measure
and control the thickness of the
substance.

front:
How is gamma radiation used in the
treatment of cancer? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Gamma radiation is used in the
treatment of cancer in the process of
radiotherapy. Gamma radiation can
damage cells and tissues so this can be
used to target cancer cells. Gamma rays
can penetrate the body to reach the
cancer cells, but the beams must be
emitted from different angles to reduce
the damage to healthy tissues.

front:
What are the three effects of ionising
nuclear radiation on living things?
back:
The three effects of ionising nuclear
radiation that you need to know are:
cell death (and therefore tissue
damage)
mutations
cancer

front:
How does ionising radiation cause cell
mutations?
back:
Ionising radiation can remove
electrons from the atoms that make up
DNA and therefore change the
structure of the molecule. A structural
change in DNA can lead to mutated
cells. Mutated cells usually either die or
get destroyed by the immune system,
but some mutations can cause cells to
replicate uncontrollably and lead to
cancer.

front: How is radioactive waste disposed of?
back:
Radioactive waste is disposed of by:
containing it in marked containers
burying it underground
leaving it undisturbed for
thousands of years

front:
How should radioactive samples be
handled? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Radioactive samples should be handled
by:
storing the sample encased in lead
using gloves and tongues to move
the sample
wearing protective clothing
keeping the sample at a distance
from the body
minimising the exposure time
washing hands after to avoid
contamination

front:
Define the term dose in relation to
radioactive substances. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
A dose is the amount of radiation
received by a person. It is measured in
sieverts (Sv).

front:
What could over-exposure to nuclear
radiation lead to?
back:
Over-exposure to nuclear radiation
could lead to radiation poisoning.

front: What is a dosemeter?
back:
A dosemeter is a device worn by
people who work with radiation that
measures the amount of radiation
received.

front:
True or False?
The Earth completes one full rotation in
approximately 24 hours.
back:
True.
It takes approximately 24 hours for the
Earth to rotate once on its axis.

front:
What causes one Earth year to have 365
days?
back:
One Earth year has 365 days because it
takes the Earth 365 days to complete
one orbit around the Sun.

front: What causes day and night on Earth?
back:
Day and night are caused by the
rotation of the Earth on its axis.

front:
True or False?
The seasons are caused by the tilt of
the Earth on its axis only.
back:
False.
The seasons are caused by the tilt of the
Earth on its axis and its orbit around
the Sun once every 365 days.

front: Define the term equinox.
back:
Equinox occurs when the hours of day
and night are the same in both
hemispheres.

front: Define the term summer solstice.
back:
Summer solstice is the longest day of
the year when the Sun reaches its
highest point above the horizon.

front:
True or False?
When it is the summer solstice in the
southern hemisphere, it is the winter
solstice in the northern hemisphere.
back:
True.
When it is the summer solstice in the
southern hemisphere, it is the winter
solstice in the northern hemisphere.

front:
True or False?
The Moon produces its own light.
back:
False.
The Moon shines with light reflected
from the Sun, it does not produce its
own light.

front: Define the term full Moon.
back:
A full Moon occurs when the Moon is on
the opposite side of the Earth from the
Sun and appears as a whole circle.

front:
List two reasons why the phases of the
Moon occur.
back:
The phases of the Moon occur because:
1. The Moon orbits the Earth once every
28 days.
2. The Moon reflects light from the Sun.

front:
List five objects that make up the Solar
System.
back:
Five objects that make up the Solar
System are:
1. The Sun
2. Eight planets
3. Satellites (natural and artificial)
4. Dwarf planets
5. Asteroids and comets

front:
State the names of the planets in order
of increasing distance from the Sun.
back:
The planets in order of increasing
distance from the Sun are:
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter,
Saturn, Uranus, Neptune

front: What is an asteroid?
back:
An asteroid is a small rocky object which
orbits the Sun.

front: Where is the asteroid belt located?
back:
The asteroid belt is located between
Mars and Jupiter.

front: What are comets made of?
back: Comets are made of dust and ice.

front:
True or False?
All objects in the Solar System orbit
around the Sun.
back:
False.
Planets, dwarf planets, asteroids and
comets orbit around the Sun, whereas
satellites, such as moons, orbit around
planets.

front:
What is the difference between natural
and artificial satellites?
back:
A natural satellite is a non-manmade
object that orbits a planet, such as a
moon.
An artificial satellite is a manmade
object that can orbit any object in
space.

front:
How does the orbital radius of a planet
change with increasing distance from
the Sun? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The orbital radius of a planet increases
with increasing distance from the Sun.

front:
How does the orbital period of a planet
change with increasing distance from
the Sun? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The orbital period of a planet increases
with increasing distance from the Sun.

front:
True or False?
The outer planets are denser than the
inner planets. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
The inner planets are denser than the
outer planets.

front:
True or False?
Neptune is the coldest planet.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
The surface temperature of a planet
tends to decrease with distance from
the Sun (with the exception of Venus).
Neptune is the furthest planet from the
Sun, therefore, it is the coldest planet.

front:
True or False?
The surface gravity on Saturn is greater
than on Earth. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
Surface gravity depends on the mass of
a planet.
Values of surface gravity are greater on
the giant outer planets than on the
small inner planets.
Therefore, the surface gravity on Saturn
is greater than on Earth.

front:
True or False?
The inner planets are small and rocky.
The outer planets are large and
gaseous.
back:
True.
The inner planets (Mercury, Venus,
Earth, Mars) are small and rocky.
The outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn,
Uranus, Neptune) are large and
gaseous.

front: What is an accretion disc?
back:
An accretion disc is a rotating disc of
dust and gas that forms around an
object, such as the Sun during its
formation.

front:
According to the accretion model, what
caused the differences in the size and
composition of the inner and outer
planets?
back:
According to the accretion model:
The inner planets are small and
rocky because a small proportion of
heavy elements were solid closer to
the Sun
The outer planets are large and
gaseous because a large proportion
of light elements were solid further
from the Sun

front:
True or False?
Light travels instantaneously across
large distances.
back:
False.
Light travels at a constant speed of 3 ×
108 m/s, therefore, it takes time for light
to travel any distance.

front:
What equation can be used to calculate
the time taken for light to travel a
certain distance?
back:
The equation that can be used to
calculate the time taken for light to
travel a certain distance is:

time = speed of light

front:
State the meaning of gravitational
field strength .
back:
Gravitational field strength is the
strength of the gravitational pull
exerted by an object, such as a planet
or moon, on another object on or near
its surface.

front:
What does the strength of a
gravitational field around a planet
depend on?
back:
The strength of a gravitational field
around a planet depends on:
the mass of the planet
the distance from the planet

front:
On which planet in the Solar System
would your weight be the heaviest?
back:
The greater the gravitational field
strength of a planet, the greater the
measured weight of a person standing
on its surface.
Therefore, your weight would be the
greatest on Jupiter, as this is the largest
(most massive) planet.

front:
The greater the mass of a planet, the
gravitational field at its surface.
back:
The greater the mass of a planet, the
the strength of thegreater the strength of the gravitational
field at its surface.

front:
As the distance from a planet
, the strength of the gravitational field
decreases.
back:
As the distance from a planet
increases, the strength of the
gravitational field decreases.

front:
True or False?
Gravitational field strength is constant
at the surface of a given planet.
back:
True.
Gravitational field strength is constant
at the surface of a given planet, but it
decreases with distance above the
planet's surface.

front:
In which direction does the gravitational
force of an orbiting body act?
back:
The gravitational force exerted on an
orbiting body acts towards the centre
of the larger body it is orbiting.

front:
True or False?
The strength of the Sun's gravitational
field increases as the distance from the
Sun increases. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
The strength of the Sun's gravitational
field decreases as the distance from
the Sun increases.

front:
What happens to the orbital speed of a
planet as the distance from the Sun
increases? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The orbital speed of a planet decreases
as the distance from the Sun increases.

front:
Define the term orbital speed.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Orbital speed is the average speed of an
object as it orbits around a larger
object.

front:
True or False?
When planets and satellites orbit larger
bodies, they move in approximately
circular paths. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
When a planet orbits the Sun or a
satellite orbits a planet, they move in
approximately circular paths.

front:
State the equation for calculating orbital
speed in terms of distance and time.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The equation for calculating orbital
speed is sp eed = distan ce
time

front:
Define the term orbital period.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Orbital period is the time it takes an
object to complete one full orbit around
another object.

front:
What is the orbital period of the Earth?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The orbital period of the Earth is 365
days, the time it takes to complete one
orbit around the Sun.

front:
True or False?
The orbital radius is measured from the
surface of the orbiting body. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
False.
The orbital radius is always taken from
the centre of mass of the orbiting body.

front:
What is the distance travelled by an
object moving in circular motion in one
orbit? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The distance travelled by an object
moving in circular motion is equal to the
circumference of the orbit = 2πr , where
r is the radius of the orbit.

front:
True or False?
An object in a circular orbit has a
constant orbital radius. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
An object in a circular orbit has a
constant orbital radius.

front:
State the equation for orbital speed v,
in terms of orbital radius r and time t.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The equation for orbital speed is
v = 2πr
T
Where:
v = orbital speed, measured in m/s
r = orbital radius, measured in m
T = orbital period, measured in s

front:
True or False?
The orbital radius of a satellite in orbit
around the Earth is equal to:
radius of the Earth + height above the
Earth's surface
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
The orbital radius of a satellite orbiting
the Earth is r = R + h
Where:
r = orbital radius of the satellite,
measured in m
R = radius of the Earth, measured
in m
h = height above the Earth's
surface, measured in m

front:
True or False?
The orbits of planets, minor planets and
comets are elliptical. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
The orbits of planets, minor planets and
comets are elliptical.

front:
Which type of object in the Solar System
has the most elongated elliptical orbit?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Comets have the most elongated
elliptical orbits in the Solar System.

front:
True or False?
The Sun is at the centre of an elliptical
orbit. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
When a body moves in a circular orbit,
the larger body will be at the centre of
the circle.
When a body moves in an elliptical
orbit, the larger body will be at one of
the two foci of the ellipse.
Therefore, the Sun is not at the centre
of an elliptical orbit.

front:
How does the speed of a comet change
as it approaches the Sun? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
As a comet approaches the Sun it
speeds up.

front:
In terms of conservation of energy, why
does the speed of a comet change as it
approaches the Sun? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
In terms of conservation of energy,
when a comet approaches the Sun, it
gains kinetic energy and loses
gravitational potential energy. This
causes it to speed up.

front:
What two elements is the Sun mostly
composed of?
back:
The two elements the Sun is mostly
composed of are hydrogen and helium.

front:
True or False?
The Sun is a planet which makes up
over 99% of the mass of the Solar
System.
back:
False.
The Sun is a star which makes up over
99% of the mass of the Solar System.

front:
Name the main types of radiation
emitted by the Sun.
back:
The main types of radiation emitted by
the Sun are in the infrared, visible and
ultraviolet regions of the
electromagnetic spectrum.

front:
What is nuclear fusion? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
Nuclear fusion is the joining of two
smaller nuclei to form one larger
nucleus, releasing a large amount of
energy in the process.

front:
Where do nuclear reactions take place
in stars? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
Nuclear reactions take place in the
centres (cores) of stars.

front:
How is the Sun powered? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
The Sun is powered by the nuclear
fusion of hydrogen into helium.

front: What is the Milky Way?
back:
The Milky Way is a galaxy containing
billions of stars, including our Sun.

front:
What is the difference between a
galaxy and the Universe?
back:
A galaxy is a large collection of stars,
whereas the Universe is made up of
billions of galaxies.

front: Define a light-year.
back:
A light-year is the distance travelled by
light in one year.

front:
What is the diameter of the Milky Way
in light years?
back:
The diameter of the Milky Way is 100
000 light years.

front:
How many metres are there in one
light-year? (Extended Tier Only)
back: There are 9.5 × 1015 m in one light-year.

front:
True or False?
All stars form from a cloud of dust and
gas which becomes a protostar and
then a stable star. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
True.
All stars follow the same initial stages in
their life-cycle:
1. Nebula (cloud of dust and gas)
2. Protostar
3. Stable star
The stages that follow depend on the
mass of the stable star that forms.

front:
When does a protostar become a stable
star? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
A protostar becomes a stable star when
nuclear fusion reactions are initiated in
its core and the inward force of gravity
is balanced by the outward pressure
from the fusion reactions.

front:
What forces, including their direction,
act when a star is in a stable state?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The forces acting on a star in a stable
state are:
1. Inward gravitational force
2. Outward pressure due to energy
released by fusion

front:
True or False?
Nuclear fusion provides the pressure
that prevents stars from collapsing
under gravity. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
The thermal pressure provided by
nuclear fusion reactions prevents stars
from collapsing under gravity.

front:
Name the stages, in the correct order,
in the life cycle of a star similar to the
Sun. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The stages, in the correct order, in the
life cycle of a star similar to the Sun are:
1. Nebula (cloud of dust and gas)
2. Protostar
3. Stable star
4. Red giant
5. Planetary nebula
6. White dwarf
7. Black dwarf

front:
When does a stable star turn into a red
giant? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
A stable star turns into a red giant when
hydrogen in the star's core begins to
run out and the star begins to fuse
helium into heavier elements.

front:
True or False?
A high mass star will eventually explode
as a supernova and become a white
dwarf. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
A high mass star will eventually explode
as a supernova and become a neutron
star or a black hole.

front: What is the Doppler effect ?
back:
The Doppler effect is the change in
wavelength or frequency of a wave due
to the relative motion between the
source and the observer.

front:
True or False?
The Doppler effect applies to sound
waves only.
back:
False.
The Doppler effect applies to both
sound waves and light waves.

front:
True or False?
Waves emitted by a stationary object
have a constant wavelength.
back:
True.
When an object emits waves, the
wavefronts spread out symmetrically.
This means the wavelength of the
waves is constant.

front:
True or False?
The frequency of a wave emitted by a
moving object increases if the object is
moving away from an observer.
back:
False.
If an object moves away from an
observer, the waves spread out, so the
wavelength increases and the
frequency decreases.

front: What is redshift?
back:
Redshift is the increase in the observed
wavelength of a light source when it
moves away from an observer.

front: What is blueshift?
back:
Blueshift is the decrease in the
observed wavelength of a light source
when it moves towards an observer.

front:
Which end of the light spectrum has a
higher frequency, red or blue?
back:
The blue end of the light spectrum has
a higher frequency.

front:
How can astronomers determine if the
light from a distant galaxy is
redshifted?
back:
Astronomers can determine if the light
from a distant galaxy is redshifted by:
Comparing the light spectra of a
distant galaxy and an object on
Earth (or close to Earth, such as the
Sun)
If the lines from the distant galaxy
appear closer to the red end of the
spectrum, then the light has been
redshifted

front:
True or False?
The greater the distance to a galaxy, the
greater the redshift observed.
back:
True.
The greater the distance to a galaxy, the
greater the redshift observed, indicating
that the galaxy is moving away faster.

front: What is the Big Bang theory?
back:
The Big Bang theory states the Universe
originated from a very small region that
was extremely hot and dense, which
has been expanding and cooling for
approximately 13.8 billion years.

front:
True or False?
The Big Bang theory states that the
Universe began from a single point.
back:
True.
According to the Big Bang theory, the
Universe began from a very small
region that was extremely hot and
dense.

front:
True or False?
The Universe is currently contracting.
back:
False.
The Universe is currently expanding, as
evidenced by the redshift of distant
galaxies.

front:
What does the observation of redshift
from distant galaxies imply about the
Universe?
back:
The observation of redshift from distant
galaxies implies that the Universe is
expanding.

front:
How does galactic redshift provide
evidence for the Big Bang theory?
back:
Galactic redshift refers to the
observation that light from distant
galaxies is shifted toward longer, redder
wavelengths.
This indicates that distant galaxies are
moving away from Earth.
This provides evidence that the
Universe must be expanding, which
means that galaxies must have been
closer together in the past.

front:
What are the two main pieces of
evidence for the Big Bang theory?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The main evidence for the Big Bang
theory comes from:
1. Galactic redshift
2. Cosmic microwave background
radiation (CMBR)

front:
What is cosmic microwave
background radiation (CMBR)?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
CMBR is a type of electromagnetic
radiation with a wavelength in the
microwave region. It is observed to be
very uniform at all points in space.

front:
What is the origin of CMBR? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
The CMBR was originally emitted at the
time of the Big Bang when the Universe
was formed.

front:
How does CMBR provide evidence for
the Big Bang theory? (Extended Tier
Only) which has been redshifted to the
back:
CMBR provides evidence for the Big
Bang Theory because it represents
remnant radiation from the Big Bang
microwave region of the
electromagnetic spectrum.

front:
True or False?
CMBR is completely uniform in
temperature. (Extended Tier Only)
back:
True.
CMBR has minuscule temperature
fluctuations on the order of 0.00001 K,
implying that objects in the Universe are
uniformly spread out.

front:
How can the distance to a galaxy be
estimated? (Extended Tier Only)
back:
The distance to a galaxy can be
estimated from the brightness
measurements of a standard candle
(an object of known brightness) called a
supernova in the galaxy being
observed.

front:
Define Hubble's Law. (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
Hubble's Law states that the speed of
recession of a galaxy is directly
proportional to its distance from Earth.

front:
Define the Hubble Constant.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The Hubble constant (H0) is the ratio of
the speed of recession of a galaxy to its
distance from the Earth.

front:
Express Hubble's Law as an equation.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
Hubble's Law can be expressed as the
equation v = H 0d
Where:
v = the speed of recession of the
galaxy, measured in km/s
H = the Hubble constant (2.2 × 10–
18 per second)
d = the distance to the galaxy,
measured in km

front:
What is the currently accepted value of
the Hubble constant? (Extended Tier
Only)
back:
The currently accepted value of the
Hubble constant (H0) is 2.2 × 10–18 per
second.

front:
True or False?
The further away a galaxy is, the faster
it is moving away from us. (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
True.
Hubble's Law shows that the further
away a galaxy is from Earth, the faster
it is moving away from us.

back:
The term 1 represents the age of the

Universe has been expanding.

front:
True or False?
According to Hubble's Law, if Galaxy A is
twice as far away as Galaxy B, then
Galaxy B must be moving away from
Earth at twice the speed of Galaxy A.
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
False.
Hubble's Law states that the distance to
a galaxy (d ) and the speed it moves
away from Earth (v) are directly
proportional to each other.
Therefore, if Galaxy A is twice as far
away as Galaxy B, Galaxy A must be
moving away at twice the speed of
Galaxy B.

front:
What is the estimated age of the
Universe based on Hubble's Law?
(Extended Tier Only)
back:
The estimated age of the Universe
based on Hubble's Law is about 13.7
billion years.

front:
How can the age of the Universe be
determined from a graph of recessional
velocity against distance? (Extended
Tier Only)
back:
The age of the Universe can be
determined from a graph of recessional
velocity against distance because it is
equal to the gradient of the graph.
